cases.notes: LocaleMatcher:118 TRUE -- the absent header. Spelled as an explicit JSON null rather than by omitting the key, because plan v7 section 3.5 types the JS parameter `string | null | undefined` and both spellings must land on this row; ingest refuses the omitted key so the two can never be conflated. DISCRIMINATING: a port without the null guard dereferences the header and throws (TypeError) where Java answers ja, and a throw on this operation is by itself a defect.

LocaleMatcher:120 TRUE -- the whitespace-only header. HONEST LIMIT, measured rather than assumed: against Java this branch is COVERAGE-ONLY. With the check deleted, "   " normalizes to "" and :125 returns the same fallback, so the two arms are indistinguishable in Java. It still discriminates at the PORT level -- a JS implementation whose own parser throws on a blank header and which lacks an equivalent guard surfaces a throw where Java answers ja -- which is why the case is authored, but the record should not claim more than that.

THE CONTROL, and every other row here is read against it. It is the only input in the family that traverses the whole method without taking a fail-soft exit: LocaleMatcher:118 FALSE, :119 FALSE, :120 FALSE, :125 FALSE, :136 FALSE, and :151's end-of-string member boundary with no trailing comma. Without it the family degenerates into 'everything returns ja' and could not tell a correct implementation from one that returns the fallback unconditionally.

LocaleMatcher:152's comma arm, :166 FALSE (the empty member is dropped) and :167 TRUE (a comma is re-inserted before the second survivor). EMPTY LIST ELEMENT removal is the reason the normalizer exists. DISCRIMINATING: measured that LanguageRange.parse("fr,,de") raw THROWS IllegalArgumentException("range="), so a port that does not drop the empty element answers ja where Java answers fr. The corpus already carries this exact header as browser-chooser.malformed.empty-list-element, partitioned informational because the JDK parser throws on it before the library is reached; this operation is what turns that informational curiosity into required portable behavior.

LocaleMatcher:167 FALSE reached after a member was dropped -- the first SURVIVOR is not the first member, so nothing may be prepended. DISCRIMINATING: a port that appends the separator unconditionally produces ",fr", and measured, LanguageRange.parse(",fr") throws, so such a port answers ja where Java answers fr.

The VIRTUAL member after a final comma: zero-length, so :166 takes its FALSE arm and nothing is appended. Read against accept-language.control.plain-header-matches, which differs only in the trailing comma. HONEST LIMIT, and this row REDUNDANT AGAINST JAVA -- an earlier note claimed it closed :151's loop boundary and discriminated against a port that emits a trailing separator, and measurement refutes both. :151's loop-exit arm is taken by every non-null header, the control included, so this row closes nothing unique; and LanguageRange.parse("fr,") does NOT reject -- measured on the pinned JDK it returns one range, fr@1.0, because String.split drops trailing empties -- so a port that faithfully mirrors parse and emits the trailing separator still answers fr and this row cannot see that defect. It is kept rather than retired because it costs nothing and pins the trailing-comma shape as answering fr, but no disposition depends on it and the record must not bank it as discrimination.

The present-but-empty header, which is NOT the same input as the absent one: it passes :118 and is stopped at :120 by "".trim().isEmpty(). Read against accept-language.absent.null-header, which reaches the same answer down a different path. HONEST LIMIT, corrected by measurement after a reviewer challenged an earlier claim here that "both are needed because a port that treats null and \"\" as one value passes either alone": that is incoherent, because Java answers ja for BOTH inputs, so a port conflating them answers correctly on both and passes both. Measured, "" and "   " take an IDENTICAL arm set (:118 FALSE, :119 FALSE, :120 TRUE), so this row closes no arm accept-language.blank.whitespace-only does not already close, and with :120 deleted "" normalizes to "" and :125 returns the same fallback. Against Java it is COVERAGE-ONLY. Its value is at the PORT level: a JS implementation that null-checks but hands "" to a parser that throws surfaces a throw where Java answers ja.

LocaleMatcher:172 TRUE -- the tab-to-space CONVERSION inside a surviving member, and the ONLY input in this family that reaches it. The disposition for this branch prescribed the leading-tab header, which is the zh-123 trap: that tab is eaten by the :157 trim loop and the conversion arm never runs, so an author following the note literally would ship a passing case and specify nothing. MEASURED through the private normalizer: this header normalizes to "de;q=0.8,f r;q=0.9" -- a real space -- and LanguageRange.parse then strips the space and selects fr. THREE-WAY DISCRIMINATION: a port that lets the tab survive answers ja (parse throws on it), one that drops the whole malformed member answers de, and only conversion answers fr.

LocaleMatcher:119 FALSE at the boundary -- 4,094 commas plus "fr", exactly 4,096 UTF-16 code units, which is accepted and normalizes to "fr" -> fr. Read as a PAIR with accept-language.length.over-cap-four-thousand-ninety-seven, which is one code unit longer and answers ja. DISCRIMINATING TWICE: it catches the off-by-one (`>=` instead of `>`), and it catches a port that measures AFTER normalizing, because both headers normalize to the same two characters. THE DISPOSITION'S OWN PRESCRIPTION FOR THIS BRANCH DOES NOT WORK and was struck: it asked for astral characters so a byte-length port would fail, but measured, a 4,096-code-unit all-emoji header and a 4,098-code-unit one BOTH answer ja, because any non-ASCII character makes LanguageRange.parse throw into the :132 catch, which returns the very fallback the length cap returns. Byte-, code-point- and code-unit-length ports are indistinguishable on any astral header.

LocaleMatcher:119 TRUE -- 4,097 UTF-16 code units, one past the cap, rejected BEFORE normalization or parsing so parser work stays bounded independently of the parsed-range limit. Read as a pair with accept-language.length.at-cap-four-thousand-ninety-six; the pair is what discriminates, neither row alone does.

LocaleMatcher:136 TRUE -- 14 header entries that LanguageRange.parse expands to 33 ranges via the IANA equivalence table, one past MAXIMUM_LANGUAGE_RANGES. THE STRONGEST ROW IN THE FAMILY: this is the same header the corpus already carries as browser-chooser.limit.alias-expansion-crosses-thirty-two, where the identical range list through bestMatchFor(List) THROWS `IllegalArgumentException: At most 32 language ranges are supported, but received 33` (measured). Fail-soft here versus strict there, on one input, is the whole reason this entry point exists. PINNED-TABLE-DEPENDENT, as its matchFor twin already is: 14 entries expanding to exactly 33 is a property of the JDK's IANA equivalence table, which lokalized-spec pins, not of Lokalized -- a port whose table differs by one entry lands on the wrong side of a boundary that will look like a parsing bug.

LocaleMatcher:136 FALSE -- 16 header entries expanding to exactly 32 ranges, accepted and passed through whole; preferences are never truncated, so the q=0.9 preference for fr wins -> fr. The twin of accept-language.limit.thirty-three-expanded-ranges; a port that truncates to 32 instead of rejecting at 33 answers this row correctly and the other one wrong.

The :132 catch -- an exception HANDLER, not a branch, so it carries no disposition and closes nothing. Authored anyway because it is the boundary the whole fail-soft contract rests on: measured, LanguageRange.parse throws IllegalArgumentException("range=notaheader!") and Java answers ja. A port that lets its own parser's error escape produces a `thrown` row here instead of a tag.

LocaleMatcher:125 TRUE -- a header that survives :120 (",,,".trim() is not empty) and normalizes to the empty string. Also the FALSE arms of :157 (a zero-length member, so the leading-OWS scan never runs), :162 and :166. Same honest limit as the blank row: measured that LanguageRange.parse("") throws IllegalArgumentException("range=") into the :132 catch and that parse(",,,") raw returns zero ranges, so all three roads end at bestMatchFor(List.of()) and the same fallback -- against Java this is coverage, not discrimination. It discriminates against a port whose parser throws out.

The other half of the same divergence, from the opposite direction. A newline IS cut by String.trim() at :120, so the header is not blank there; it is NOT OWS at :183, so the normalizer preserves it; parse then throws -> ja. DISCRIMINATING: a JS port that trims members with a `\s`-class regex, which matches \n, answers fr. The pair with the no-break-space row pins the OWS set from both sides -- narrower than \s, and not the same set as the blank check one line above it.

THE SHARPEST JS-SPECIFIC ROW HERE, and one no disposition proposes. Java's OWS set is exactly {space, tab} (LocaleMatcher:183), while the trim at :120 is String.trim(), which cuts everything <= U+0020 -- the two are deliberately different widths. U+00A0 survives BOTH, so the member reaches LanguageRange.parse intact and parse throws (measured: `range=\u00a0fr`) -> ja. DISCRIMINATING: a JS port that trims members with String.prototype.trim(), which strips U+00A0 and U+FEFF, answers fr. Read against accept-language.ows-set.trailing-space-is-trimmed, which differs only in which whitespace character it uses.

The CONTROL half of the OWS-set pair, and the one that stops the other half from being read as 'any odd character returns the fallback'. An ASCII space is OWS, so it is trimmed and the header still answers fr.

LocaleMatcher:157's leading-OWS trim with a SPACE, and :183's first disjunct. RFC 9110 optional whitespace after a list separator is legal and must be removed before parsing: measured, LanguageRange.parse accepts this raw, so the row's force is that a port must not CORRUPT it -- and read with its tab twin it fixes exactly which two characters count as OWS.

LocaleMatcher:157's leading-OWS trim with a HORIZONTAL TAB, and :183's second disjunct. DISCRIMINATING: measured that LanguageRange.parse of this header raw THROWS IllegalArgumentException("range=\tfr"), so a port that treats only the space as OWS answers ja where Java answers fr. The corpus twin browser-chooser.malformed.horizontal-tab-ows is informational for that reason. NOTE FOR ANYONE READING THE :172 DISPOSITION: this header does NOT reach :172. Its tab is LEADING within its member and is consumed by the trim loop at :157 before the copy loop at :170 ever runs -- measured through the private normalizer, this header normalizes to "de;q=0.8,fr;q=0.9" with NO space in it. See accept-language.interior-tab.converted-to-space.

The space spelling of the trailing trim at :163, and multiple OWS characters per side rather than one. Read against accept-language.ows.tab-on-both-sides: together they establish that the trim loops are loops over the OWS SET, not single-character strips. HONEST LIMIT: measured, LanguageRange.parse accepts this header raw (2 ranges -> fr), so against Java the trim is not what decides the answer -- this row pins the loop shape -- multiple OWS characters per side -- and discriminates only against a port that CORRUPTS a member while trimming it. It does NOT uniquely close ':163's space spelling', as an earlier draft claimed: the space arm of the OWS test at :183 is also taken by accept-language.ows-set.trailing-space-is-trimmed ("fr ") and by accept-language.ows.leading-space, and :163 itself is a loop guard whose two arms carry no character spelling at all. Its tab twin, accept-language.ows.tab-on-both-sides, is the half that discriminates against Java.

LocaleMatcher:162 and :163 -- the TRAILING-trim loop, whose guard and whose isOptionalWhitespace test are separate branch points from the leading trim at :157. The first member is tab-padded on both sides. DISCRIMINATING: measured that parse of this header raw throws IllegalArgumentException("range=\tfr\t"), so a port that trims only the leading side answers ja where Java answers fr.

No per-call locale at all, so optionsFrom builds TranslationOptions.none() and localeLookupFor falls through to the instance localeSupplier -- the ambient locale, he (DefaultStrings.java:2456). Isolation must still be decided from that ambient locale, and the he template must be the one that resolves. A port that only consults an explicitly-passed locale, or that treats a missing locale as the FALLBACK locale (en) rather than the instance locale, gets both the wrong template and no marks. Authored as `get` rather than `getResult` on purpose: the oracle's getResult branch always evaluates Cardinality.supportedCardinalitiesForLocale(Locale.forLanguageTag(input.locale)) for its classifications channel, and Locale.forLanguageTag(null) throws, so a locale-less getResult would record an oracle NullPointerException instead of a translation.

The other half of the default. A Hebrew value dropped into an English template is NOT isolated under RTL_LOCALES, because shouldApplyBidiIsolation looks at the resolved locale's script (BidiUtils.localeUsesRightToLeftScript) and never at the value's own direction. A port that defaulted to ALWAYS, or that sniffed the VALUE for RTL characters instead of the locale, emits isolate marks here and fails. Paired with the sibling case this proves the default is RTL_LOCALES and not NONE or ALWAYS.

Same operation and same expected shape as the ambient case, with the locale passed explicitly. Authored as its pair so the ambient case is read against an identical-operation comparand rather than against a getResult sibling: if the two `get` translations agree, the ambient path really did select he; if a port resolved the ambient call against en they diverge in both the template text and the isolate marks.

Pins the library DEFAULT. No bidiIsolation is configured anywhere, so DefaultStrings.java:477 falls back to DEFAULT_BIDI_ISOLATION = RTL_LOCALES (:73/:80). Hebrew is the donor and Hebr is in GeneratedCldrLocaleData.RTL_SCRIPTS, so the Latin name must be wrapped. A port whose default is NONE returns a bare 'Sarah' here, and this is the only case in the family that catches that without any explicit mode being set.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: get() versus getResult() on identical input: get returns the same isolated interpolated key that getResult puts in result.translation, because get is getResult(...).getTranslation() (DefaultStrings.java:640-643). Authored as a pair with the getResult twin so a port cannot implement the two entry points with divergent isolation.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

thrown.message: No match for 'Farewell {{name}}' was found for locale 'en'.

cases.notes: The throwing path under ALWAYS, authored as `get` because that is where the handler's THROW_EXCEPTION response actually escapes -- getResult on this same input would return a result object. The failure reason is MISSING_TRANSLATION with no cause, so throwExceptionFor (DefaultStrings.java:3196-3212) falls past its rethrow-the-cause branch and constructs a MissingTranslationException whose message is the one built at :742, carrying the RAW key with its literal '{{name}}'. It never touches the interpolator or BidiUtils. A port that isolated eagerly, or that interpolated the key before constructing the diagnostic, puts directional controls inside an exception message, which is unreadable in logs.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: Same fixture, same key, same ALWAYS mode -- only the per-call handler differs, and now the key IS interpolated and the value IS isolated. Pins that the handler's RESPONSE, not the mode, decides whether isolation happens at all on the failure path, and that a per-call handler replaces the instance handler (DefaultStrings.java:684). getResult twin of the get case below.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: The RETURN_STRING branch returns translationFailureResponse.getTranslation() verbatim into the TranslationResult (DefaultStrings.java:757-759); it never reaches interpolateFailureKey, so the '{{name}}' inside the substitute is neither interpolated nor isolated even though the instance is set to ALWAYS. A port that funnelled every failure response through the same interpolation path emits an isolated 'Sarah' here.

Isolation applies ONLY to caller-supplied values. In interpolateTemplate the file-defined branch (placeholderBindings.containsKey) never calls shouldApplyBidiIsolation; only the else branch reading immutableContext does (DefaultStrings.java:1365-1371). So under ALWAYS the generated {{title}} ('Ms.', which came out of the strings file) is bare while {{name}} and {{city}} are wrapped, in one string. A port that isolates every interpolated slot uniformly wraps the translator's own text -- the single most likely bidi bug in a port, and this is the only case in the corpus that catches it.

Control that makes the mixed case readable: with NONE the identical lookup produces the fully bare string, so the marks present in the sibling are attributable to the two caller-supplied slots specifically rather than to anything about this template or this gender selection.

Instance-level ALWAYS isolates in an LTR locale, which is the whole point of the mode: it protects an RTL value embedded in an LTR translation, the inverse of the case RTL_LOCALES handles. shouldApplyBidiIsolation returns true unconditionally for ALWAYS (DefaultStrings.java:1427-1428). Under the default this lookup emits no marks, so the case discriminates instance ALWAYS from an ignored instance setting.

ALWAYS means always: a pure-Latin value in a pure-Latin locale is still wrapped, because nothing in shouldApplyBidiIsolation or BidiUtils.isolate inspects the value's direction. This kills any implementation that treats isolation as an optimization to be skipped when 'nothing could reorder'. Exact string comparisons downstream depend on the marks being present here.

Per-call override in the restrictive direction, the mirror of instance-none.per-call-always-overrides. Together the two prove the per-call value replaces the instance value in BOTH directions rather than only being able to widen or only being able to narrow.

A per-call RTL_LOCALES must be able to turn OFF isolation that the instance's ALWAYS would have applied, because the resolved locale is LTR. A port that treated the instance setting as a floor -- 'at least as much isolation as configured' -- emits marks here and fails.

Companion to the narrowing case: the same per-call RTL_LOCALES over the same instance ALWAYS still isolates when the resolved locale is RTL. Without this pair the narrowing case could be satisfied by a port that reads a per-call RTL_LOCALES as NONE.

Per-call override in the permissive direction. options.getBidiIsolation().orElse(getBidiIsolation()) at DefaultStrings.java:683 means the per-call value REPLACES the instance value rather than intersecting with it. Same fixture and same input as the previous case, opposite output: a port that ignores per-call bidiIsolation, or that ANDs it with the instance setting, produces the unisolated string.

Control that makes the previous case load-bearing. The identical per-call override on an LTR locale must NOT isolate, proving the override installs the RTL_LOCALES policy and is not just a truthy 'turn isolation on' flag. A port that mapped any non-NONE per-call value onto ALWAYS passes the previous case and fails this one.

RTL_LOCALES supplied per-call over an instance NONE. Distinct from the ALWAYS override because it must re-enable the script test rather than force isolation on: it isolates only because the resolved locale happens to be Hebrew. Needed so the next case can show the same override producing the opposite answer for an LTR locale.

Instance-level NONE must beat the locale's RTL-ness: shouldApplyBidiIsolation returns false for NONE before ever asking about the script (DefaultStrings.java:1424-1426). Under the library default this same lookup isolates, so the case is a real discriminator. A port that hard-coded 'isolate when the resolved locale is RTL' -- which the four bidi cases already in the evaluation-locale family would let it get away with, since that family cannot set a mode -- fails here.

Control isolating the variable: the same Arabic entry requested directly, with no fallback in play, must also isolate (attemptedLocales is just [ar] rather than [en, ar], which the result channel records). Establishes that the isolation in the fallback case belongs to the donor's script and not to the act of falling back.

The clause built the other way round: English is requested, the en catalog lacks the key, the Arabic fallback locale supplies it (localeFallbackCandidates appends getFallbackLocale(), DefaultStrings.java:2489), and under the default RTL_LOCALES the Latin name IS wrapped because the DONOR is Arabic. Exactly inverts the rtl-request-ltr-donor case. A port keying off the requested locale drops the marks here -- and dropping them is the failure mode that actually garbles rendering, since a Latin run inside an Arabic sentence is what reorders.

ALWAYS on the same input reaches the same isolated output as the default did, but for a different reason -- unconditional rather than via the donor's script. Recorded so all three modes are pinned on this direction of the clause, and so a port cannot pass the default-mode case by implementing ALWAYS everywhere: the NONE sibling forbids that.
NONE suppresses the donor-driven isolation. Same fixture, same input, opposite output from the previous case, so the mode's effect is separable from the donor locale's.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en, ar]

cases.notes: Mirror of the returned-key asymmetry. The key exists in no catalog, so interpolateFailureKey uses the REQUESTED locale (en) and does not isolate -- even though this instance's fallback locale is Arabic and every resolved lookup on this fixture does isolate. A port that used the fallback locale, or the last attempted locale, on the failure path wraps the value here.

The two isolate characters count against maximumInterpolatedOutputCharacters. Traced: StringInterpolator emits '[' (1 character), then hands BoundedIsolatedValue.render a remaining budget of 10 - 1 = 9; isolate builds FSI + 6 + PDI = 8, which fits; the interpolator appends it (9) and then ']' (10). Exactly on the configured 10, so the lookup must succeed. Pins the off-by-one against the next case.

failures.causeMessage: Interpolated output exceeds the maximum of 10 characters
failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Wrap.Value' for locale 'en'. Reason: RESOLUTION_FAILURE. Attempted locales: [en]

failureCause.message: Interpolated output exceeds the maximum of 10 characters

cases.notes: One character more and the isolated output overruns: the rendered value is FSI + 7 + PDI = 9, the interpolator is at 10 after appending it, and the closing ']' trips an appendChecked, throwing IllegalStateException("Interpolated output exceeds the maximum of 10 characters"). BidiUtils and StringInterpolator raise the identical type and message, so the case pins the failure, not which appendChecked saw it. getResult catches it as a RESOLUTION_FAILURE and the default return-key handler takes over, so the result is a RETURNED_KEY whose failure record carries the cause identity -- that is what distinguishes this from an ordinary missing translation. A port that applied the limit to the pre-isolation value silently succeeds here and emits an over-budget string.

Idempotence observed THROUGH the budget, which no other case can do. The value is already FSI/PDI-wrapped and eight characters long; isIsolated returns true and isolate() returns the same String, adding nothing, so '[' + 8 + ']' lands exactly on 10 and the lookup succeeds. A port that re-wraps a pre-isolated value would produce ten characters here and blow the limit -- turning a silent double-wrap into an observable failure, where the value-shapes fixture (with the default 262144 limit) could only observe it as a longer string.

The discriminator for the whole limit group: the identical value under the identical limit RESOLVES once isolation is switched off, because '[abcdefg]' is nine characters and fits inside 10. Same fixture, same key, same limit; the mode is the only variable -- so a port cannot pass the failing sibling by tightening its budget accounting generally.

The section 8.3 clause case, and the family's sharpest finding. Arabic is requested; the ar catalog lacks the key; the English fallback entry supplies it. DefaultStrings.java:713 hands getInternal the candidateLocale (en), and that is the locale shouldApplyBidiIsolation sees at :1367 -- so under the default RTL_LOCALES an RTL LOOKUP SERVED BY A FALLBACK-LOCALE ENTRY IS NOT ISOLATED. A port that keys isolation off the requested locale wraps the value here and corrupts every exact comparison on the fallback path. The existing evaluation-locale family records this same observation under the default; this fixture exists so the next two cases can vary the MODE on the identical input, which that family cannot do.

The clause's core input through the OTHER entry point. get() is getResult(...).getTranslation() (DefaultStrings.java:640-643), so the donor rule must produce the identical bare string on both. Authored because a port is free to implement get() as its own resolution path; if it applied isolation from the requested locale there while getResult used the donor, only a paired case catches the divergence.

Separates the MODE from the LOCALE on the exact input the clause is about. Identical request and donor as the default-mode case, ALWAYS instead of the default, and the value is now wrapped. This proves that case's bare output is a consequence of the donor-locale rule and not of isolation being unreachable on fallback paths at all.

The third mode on the clause's input, completing NONE/ALWAYS/RTL_LOCALES coverage for an RTL request served by an LTR donor. Its output necessarily coincides with the default-mode case -- that agreement is the proposition: a port cannot 'fix' the default-mode case by special-casing NONE, because both configurations are recorded as producing the same bare string while ALWAYS on the same input does not.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: ALWAYS on the failure-key path with an LTR requested locale. Completes the three-mode matrix for the returned-key channel and shows that the channel is not hard-wired to RTL_LOCALES semantics. Under the default this same request emits no marks.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'ar'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ar, en]

cases.notes: The mode is consulted on the failure-key path too, not just on the resolved path: interpolateFailureKey takes the same bidiIsolation argument (DefaultStrings.java:1394) and calls the same shouldApplyBidiIsolation (:1406). Without this a port could hard-code 'the returned key is always isolated for an RTL request' and still pass the previous case.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell {{name}}' for locale 'ar'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ar, en]

cases.notes: The asymmetry. This key is in no catalog, so there is no donor and DefaultStrings.java:754 hands interpolateFailureKey the REQUESTED locale, whose script test at :1406 sees Arabic and isolates. Same fixture, same mode, same value, same requested locale as the clause case above -- and the opposite answer, purely because one path resolved an entry and the other did not. A port that unifies the two paths on a single locale is wrong on exactly one of them.

The discriminator for the other branch of localeUsesRightToLeftScript: a non-empty getScript() short-circuits the likely-subtag lookup, so ar-Latn tests Latn, is LTR, and is NOT isolated under the default RTL_LOCALES. Same primary language as the previous case, opposite answer, and ar-Latn is a loaded catalog so it resolves to itself and the donor rule cannot confound the reading. A port that decided RTL-ness from a hard-coded language list (ar, he, fa, ur) rather than from the script wraps the value here and fails.

Proves the ar-Latn non-isolation is the script test's doing and not a tiebreaker or catalog quirk of this fixture: forcing ALWAYS on the identical lookup isolates, and the translation text stays the ar-Latn one, so the same entry was selected both times.

'ar' carries no script subtag, so BidiUtils.localeUsesRightToLeftScript takes the script.length() == 0 branch and asks CldrLocaleData.likelySubtagFor (ar -> ar-Arab-EG), then tests Arab against RTL_SCRIPTS. A port that only looked at an explicit script subtag would find none and treat plain 'ar' as LTR, silently disabling isolation for the single most common RTL locale tag.

Idempotence. BidiUtils.isIsolated returns true for a value that starts with an isolate initiator, stays at depth > 0 until the final character, and ends balanced; isolate() then returns the String unchanged. A port that wraps unconditionally emits a doubly-isolated value; renderers tolerate it but exact comparisons do not.

The initiator set is {LRI U+2066, RLI U+2067, FSI U+2068}, not FSI alone (BidiUtils.isIsolateInitiator). A value already wrapped in LRI/PDI must be left alone. A port that only recognized FSI as pre-isolation double-wraps here while passing the FSI case.
Third member of the initiator set, RLI U+2067, with an RTL payload. Completes the recognition table so a port cannot pass by hard-coding two of the three initiators.

An RTL value in an LTR locale under ALWAYS -- the configuration the mode exists for. Same marks as the Latin case: BidiUtils.isolate always opens with FIRST_STRONG_ISOLATE, so a port that chose LRI or RLI based on the value's own direction produces different bytes here.

The length-2 boundary of isIsolated (its guard is valueLength < 2). An empty FSI/PDI pair is already isolated and must survive untouched. A port whose pre-isolation check required at least one character between the marks re-wraps it.

isolate() returns "" from its valueLength == 0 early return, so an empty caller value contributes NO marks at all even under ALWAYS -- note that the empty string is still non-null, so it does reach BidiUtils.isolatedValue. A port that wraps unconditionally emits an FSI/PDI pair around nothing, which is invisible on screen and breaks every exact-string assertion involving an optional field.

Starts with FSI and is balanced overall, but depth returns to 0 before the last character, so isIsolated returns false at its `isolateDepth == 0 && i < valueLength - 1` guard and the whole thing is wrapped again with the inner pair preserved. The sharpest test of the idempotence check: a naive 'starts with an initiator and ends with PDI' test passes the earlier cases and fails this one, leaving 'b' outside any isolate.

A value that is itself mixed-direction. The library still emits a single FSI/PDI pair around the whole value and does not segment it or insert marks at the direction change. A port that tried to be clever about internal runs emits a different string.

Isolation is applied to every caller-supplied value, not only to strings: BoundedIsolatedValue.render sends a non-CharSequence through String.valueOf and then isolates. A port that isolated only values already typed as strings leaves numbers -- exactly the values that reorder next to RTL text -- unprotected.

failures.causeMessage: Missing value for placeholder(s) [value] in key 'Wrap.Value'
failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Wrap.Value' for locale 'en'. Reason: RESOLUTION_FAILURE. Attempted locales: [en]

failureCause.message: Missing value for placeholder(s) [value] in key 'Wrap.Value'

cases.notes: The `value != null` guard at DefaultStrings.java:1367 runs before isolation, so a null caller value is put into the interpolation context untouched; StringInterpolator then records it as UNRESOLVED and interpolateTemplate throws IllegalArgumentException("Missing value for placeholder(s) [value] in key 'Wrap.Value'"), which getResult catches as a RESOLUTION_FAILURE. A port that isolated first would produce a resolved '[⁨null⁩]' -- the word null wrapped in directional controls -- instead of a failure. The free failure channel records the reason and cause identity.

Baseline for the value-shape family: a plain value is wrapped in FSI (U+2068) and PDI (U+2069), and nothing else in the template is touched. The surrounding brackets pin that the marks go around the VALUE, not around the whole interpolated string.

The complement of the dropped-PDI case: an initiator the caller left open is closed by the library, which appends one PDI per unclosed level before the outer PDI. Not pre-isolated (depth never returns to 0, so isIsolated's final `isolateDepth == 0` test fails), so the outer FSI/PDI wrap is applied too. A port that only wrapped, without balancing, leaves an RLI open and reorders everything after the placeholder.

An unmatched PDI inside a caller value is DISCARDED, not copied through: the balancing loop appends a PDI only when isolateDepth > 0. Letting a stray PDI through would pop the isolate the library just opened and defeat the whole mechanism, so a port that treats isolation as pure concatenation is unsafe against hostile or careless input. This is the injection-resistance case.

Control for the previous case: with isolation off the stray PDI passes through verbatim, because the dropping happens inside BidiUtils.isolate and nowhere else -- with NONE the value never becomes a BoundedIsolatedValue and reaches StringInterpolator as a plain CharSequence. Proves the library does not sanitize directional controls in general; a port that added a global scrubbing step would pass the dropping case and fail this one.

Both sides of one equivalence class in the same header at DIFFERENT weights. MEASURED, and NOT what a group-maximum rule would give: the parser drops the later duplicate entirely and applies the FIRST occurrence's weight to the whole class, so the emitted requestedLanguageRanges is two members both carrying 0.9 and the explicitly written 0.4 vanishes. Paired with the mirror below, which is the same two ranges in the other order and reports the other weight.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('art-lojban') already normalizes to jbo.
A grandfathered art- tag, structurally unlike the i- and zh- forms above, so the family covers three distinct grandfathered shapes rather than three spellings of one.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('i-klingon') already normalizes to tlh, so this asserts the port's grandfathered-tag canonicalization.
A grandfathered i- tag. Its equivalence lives in the IANA table, not in any subtag-structure rule, so a port deriving equivalence structurally cannot match it at all.

The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('in') already normalizes to id, so this asserts the port's own legacy-code canonicalization rather than the library's identity table.

Whole-list solver, second of the three JDK legacy codes. Included separately because the LOADER also rewrites in->id in file names, so a port could pass the loader half and fail the matcher half; all three are listed together in the loader's rewrite rule, so all three are checked rather than sampled.

The single-locale kernel for the same request. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('iw') already normalizes to he, so the kernel is handed a range identical to a loaded tag and reports a plain exact match. What this row therefore discriminates is the PORT'S OWN tag canonicalization of a JDK legacy code, not Lokalized's identity table — and the pair as a whole shows the two routes reaching one locale by two different mechanisms with different reported ranges available to them. Contrast the sgn-US pair, the one tag in this fixture that forLanguageTag leaves alone.

Whole-list solver. The range iw has no loaded source of its own; the parser materializes its pinned IANA equivalent as a SECOND member of the parsed list, and it is that member — not the one the caller wrote — that the matcher reports as the effective languageRange. A port whose parser did not expand the class matches nothing; one that expanded but reported the caller's spelling differs in the diagnostic channel.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('ji') already normalizes to yi.
Whole-list solver, third of the three JDK legacy codes the loader also rewrites.

q=0 on an ALIAS excludes the aliased source: the exclusion travels through the equivalence class to the loaded canonical tag, leaving the lower-weighted en. A port that applied exclusions before resolving equivalences still selects the aliased source.

The single-locale kernel counterpart, and the direct control for the sgn-US divergence: MEASURED, Locale.forLanguageTag('sgn-ase') DOES normalize to ase while forLanguageTag('sgn-US') does not, so these two structurally identical sgn- forms take different routes and report differently. A port that normalized both, or neither, fails exactly one of the two.
The other sgn- form for the same target, so the class is checked from both directions.

MEASURED DIVERGENCE, and the exception that makes the other .locale rows legible. Locale.forLanguageTag('sgn-US') does NOT normalize — it is the only tag in this fixture that survives intact — so this is the one kernel row that actually reaches Lokalized's own identity collection (DefaultStrings.java:2145-2159, applied at :2044-2050). Both routes select the same locale; the range-list route reports the parser-materialized canonical tag with an exact type, this route reports the caller's own sgn-us with a canonical type. Authored as a pair to record that the two solvers agree on the SELECTION and not on the DIAGNOSTICS, which the section 8.3 clause as written does not distinguish.

Whole-list solver on a sgn- prefixed sign-language equivalence. The parsed list materializes ase as a later member and the matcher reports that member, as an exact match. Paired with the .locale row, which selects the SAME locale but reports different diagnostics — the sharpest diagnostic-divergence row in the family.

The mirror that turns the row above into a falsifiable pair: same class, same two weights, opposite order, and the reported effectiveWeight is now the LOWER 0.4 while the same locale is still selected. A port that took the maximum weight across an equivalence class reports 0.9 for both rows and fails exactly one; a port that kept both entries at their written weights fails both.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-cmn') already normalizes to cmn.

The other non-canonical member of the cmn class, so the class is checked from both directions rather than one. The parsed expansion is the same three members in a different order, which is what makes the collision fixture's divergence a property of the class rather than of one spelling.

The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-guoyu') already normalizes to cmn, which is why this route has nothing to disagree with here — and why it does not move when a zh source is added in the collision fixture while the range-list route does.

Whole-list solver against a THREE-member equivalence class (cmn, zh-cmn, zh-guoyu): the parsed list carries all three and the matcher reports the canonical member. zh is deliberately not loaded in this fixture — browser-chooser-canonical-collision is the contrasting fixture where it is, and where this same range makes the two solvers disagree.

The single-locale kernel counterpart of the negative control. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-hakka') normalizes to hak, which is also unloaded, so the negative holds through a different route than the range-list one.

The negative control for the whole alias family: zh-hakka is a genuine FOUR-member equivalence class in the pinned table (the parsed list carries all four), but none of its members is loaded, so the answer is no match. Without this, every alias case could be passed by an implementation that matched aliases too eagerly.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-min-nan') already normalizes to nan.
A grandfathered THREE-subtag tag in a three-member class (nan, zh-min-nan, zh-nan). The extra subtag is where a port that truncates rather than looks up goes wrong.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-nan') already normalizes to nan.
The other non-canonical member of the nan class, reachable only through the table and not by truncating zh-min-nan.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-yue') already normalizes to yue.

Cantonese, the equivalence a naive implementation is most likely to hard-code as a zh region rather than as a distinct language. A port that treated zh-yue as zh plus a subtag would look for a zh source, which this fixture does not have.

A bare wildcard against the chooser: the reported match type is WILDCARD and the selection is en — not a zh source, and not the fallback-shaped 'first zh in the tiebreaker'. HONEST LIMIT: en is simultaneously the configured fallback AND the first supported locale in sorted order here, so this row does NOT separate the two branches of preferredLocaleForWildcard; it establishes the type and the family baseline. wildcard.prefers-fallback-over-loaded-family and the browser-chooser-wildcard-fallback cases are where those branches are actually separated.

THE COUNTERINTUITIVE HALF, and the reason the case above needs a partner. MEASURED: this does NOT exclude the bare zh source — the answer is the same one plain zh-* gives. RFC 4647 strips noninitial wildcards before categorization, so for locale zh the ranges zh-* and zh both classify as EXACT at depth 1 (DefaultStrings.java:2014-2033) and the governor sweep breaks a specificity TIE by weight (:1717-1745), leaving the q=1 member in charge. LocaleMatcher's javadoc (:55-58) states the rule as 'the most-specific matching range determines its effective quality, including a q=0 exclusion' — most specific, not any. A port implementing q=0 as set subtraction over matching locales answers zh-Hant here while still passing every other exclusion case in this family.

q=0 against an extended range, on the fixture where it bites. Compare chooser.zh-star-tiebreaker-reversed, whose request is this one minus the exclusion and which selects the OTHER source: excluding the tiebreaker-preferred locale leaves the remaining structural candidate standing, still reported as EXTENDED_RANGE. The exclusion wins because it is strictly more specific (an exact tag, depth 2) than the positive extended range that also reaches that locale.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. Both routes must produce byte-identical match blocks here, which they do — unlike the sgn-NO and zh-guoyu pairs later in this family.

zh-Hans has no loaded source but resolves to zh through CLDR parent-locale fallback, and the reported match type is neither EXACT nor the LIKELY_SUBTAG the zh-TW row above produces. A port that classified every derived match under one type would lose that distinction.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. The reported range is lowercased on BOTH routes even though the caller wrote zh-Hant, so casing is not a solver-dependent artifact.

The control for the two derived rows: when a source for the requested tag genuinely exists the match is EXACT, with the reported languageRange lowercased by the range parser. A port that reported the caller's original casing would differ here.

THE TIEBREAKER PROOF, first half. The extended range zh-* matches both loaded zh sources structurally, so preferredLocaleForRange (DefaultStrings.java:2561) must consult the configured tiebreaker order, and the reported type is EXTENDED_RANGE rather than any heuristic type.

The second half: the identical request against a fixture differing ONLY in tiebreaker order selects the other source. A port that ignored tiebreakers, or used sorted or insertion order, would return the same locale for both halves and fail exactly one. There is no single-locale counterpart — a wildcard is not expressible as a Locale.

The end-to-end half of the chooser clause: the same Accept-Language header supplied per call to getResult, so the negotiated locale is shown actually serving a translation rather than only appearing in a diagnostic. The oracle emits a standalone `match` block only when the input carries a `locale` (VectorOracle.java:224), so the negotiation is observed here through the result's own localeMatchResult, alongside lookupLocale, resolvedLocale, attemptedLocales and the translation itself.
The single-locale kernel for the same request, so the reversal control is asserted on both solvers rather than only the range-list one.

ingress-smoke pins zh-TW under tiebreaker zh:[zh, zh-Hant]. This is the same request against the REVERSED tiebreaker, and the proposition is that reversal does NOT move it: zh-TW's likely subtag is a unique candidate, so no tiebreaker is consulted. The case could have failed — the sibling zh-* cases on these same two fixtures DO move — so this is a real control, not a restatement.

The single-locale kernel counterpart. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('mo') does NOT normalize the way the iw/in/ji legacy codes do, so this route genuinely carries the caller's tag with no expansion at all — and still lands on the exact source.

mo and ro collide under CLDR canonicalization while remaining distinct loaded sources, and the parsed expansion of mo names ro at the same weight. An actual exact source must still beat a canonically equivalent one (DefaultStrings.java:1822-1826), so mo wins even though ro is the canonical tag AND is named second in the tiebreaker list. A port that canonicalized the request before looking for an exact source answers ro.
The single-locale kernel counterpart, confirming both solvers agree on a plain exact match inside the very fixture where they diverge on zh-guoyu.
The other side of the collision asked for directly, confirming both sources are individually reachable.

The single-locale kernel counterpart, which has no materialized alias member at all and still produces the identical match block. Agreement here could have failed — it does fail for zh-guoyu two rows down, in this same fixture.

An unloaded regional tag whose parsed expansion materializes an EQUAL-WEIGHT alias naming the other side of the collision (the emitted requestedLanguageRanges shows both). MEASURED: the answer is the CLDR parent of the written range, not the loaded source the alias points at. A port that let a materialized equal-weight alias claim the selection answers the other locale, and the case sits in the one fixture where both candidate answers are loaded.
The single-locale kernel counterpart. Like the zh-guoyu pair, it does not move when a zh source is added, so the pair records the divergence.
The same divergence reached through the other non-canonical member of the cmn class, so it is a property of the class rather than of one spelling.

The single-locale kernel for the same request. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('zh-guoyu') normalizes to cmn before the library sees anything, so this route has no expansion to serve at a later position and keeps the answer the alias fixture gives. The pair is the assertion, and it is only observable because the two fixtures differ by one loaded source.

THE SECOND SOLVER DIVERGENCE, and the contrast that makes it legible: the SAME range against browser-chooser-iana-aliases (where zh is not loaded) has both solvers agreeing. Add a loaded zh and this route's answer MOVES, because the parser-materialized alias member and the CLDR canonical target now name different loaded sources; the reported range becomes the caller's own spelling with a canonical type rather than the materialized member with an exact one. Paired with the .locale case, which does not move.
The single-locale kernel counterpart, asserting the Hans/Hant asymmetry holds identically on both solvers inside the fixture where they diverge on zh-guoyu.

The asymmetry that makes the two rows above meaningful: zh-Hans DOES resolve to zh through CLDR parent-locale fallback while zh-Hant does not. A port with a symmetric 'strip the script' rule matches both, and a port with no script rule at all matches neither.
The single-locale kernel counterpart of the explicit-script negative, so both routes are shown to refuse a plain zh source for a Hant request.

The script named explicitly rather than inferred from a region: still no match, because zh-Hant's CLDR parent is root and not zh. Pairs directly against collision.zh-hans-cldr-fallback-to-zh, whose only difference is the script.
The single-locale kernel counterpart of that negative.

The section 8.3 chooser row with its zh-Hant source REMOVED. zh-TW's likely subtag is Hant, and Lokalized will not serve it from a plain zh source, so the answer is no match rather than zh. A port that fell back to the primary language whenever likely-subtag inference failed answers zh here and would still pass the chooser fixture, where zh-Hant exists.
The single-locale kernel counterpart of that control; the two solvers agree here too.
The same direct-request control for the other loaded source in the conflict fixture.
The mirror, so the previous row cannot be passed by a fixed preference for one of the two.
The single-locale kernel counterpart of that control; here the two solvers do agree, which is what makes their disagreement on sgn-NO meaningful rather than a general property of this fixture.

The control: asked for directly, nsl is an exact match even though its parsed expansion also names sgn-no and sgn-nsl. Establishes that both loaded sources are individually reachable, so the divergence above is about which one wins, not about one being unreachable.

Both conflicting sources named explicitly at different weights. They must remain DISTINCT preference groups: a port that took the transitive closure of the JDK and CLDR tables would union them into one group, collapse the weights the way the alias-class rows do, and lose the caller's expressed ordering.

The other half of the divergence. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag('sgn-NO') does not normalize, so the kernel builds a single range with no parser expansion and takes the JDK identity route, selecting the source the range-list solver did not. Authored as a pair precisely so the corpus records the disagreement instead of asserting an equality that does not hold here.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CASE IN THIS FAMILY. Section 8.3 claims the range-list solver and the single-locale kernel agree; against this fixture they DO NOT, and the divergence is a direct consequence of the conflict Java documents at DefaultStrings.java:1570-1576. Through the range list, the parser expands sgn-NO into its JDK equivalents (the emitted requestedLanguageRanges shows three members) and the CLDR canonicalization of the written range decides first. Whatever this route selects, the paired .locale case selects the OTHER loaded source. A port cannot satisfy both halves with one code path.
The single-locale kernel counterpart, which agrees; Locale.forLanguageTag('sgn-nsi') normalizes to nsi.
The mirror probe for the CLDR side of the conflict; its parsed expansion is two members rather than three, which is the observable difference from sgn-nsl.

The single-locale kernel counterpart, which agrees. MEASURED: unlike sgn-NO, Locale.forLanguageTag('sgn-nsl') DOES normalize, to nsl — so the divergence above is specific to the one tag CLDR reassigns, not to sgn- forms in general, and a port that normalized sgn-NO the way it normalizes sgn-nsl would fail the divergence pair.
sgn-nsl is in the JDK equivalence class of nsl but is NOT the tag CLDR canonicalizes sgn-NO to, so it resolves unambiguously. Isolates which half of the sgn-NO conflict comes from which data source.

thrown.message: At most 32 language ranges are supported, but received 33

cases.notes: The rejecting half, and the reason the limit is documented as applying to the PARSED list rather than to comma-separated header entries: fourteen entries expand to 33 ranges and matchFor throws with Lokalized's own message naming 32 and 33. A port that counted header commas accepts this; one whose equivalence table under- or over-expands reports a different count in the message. CROSS-REFERENCE: accept-language.limit.thirty-three-expanded-ranges is this exact header through bestMatchForAcceptLanguage, which is FAIL-SOFT and answers the configured fallback where this row throws. The pair is the sharpest statement of the two entry points contract difference, on one input.

thrown.message: At most 32 language ranges are supported, but received 33

cases.notes: The same limit reached without any alias expansion at all: 33 explicit range/weight pairs, private-use-adjacent codes that match nothing. Separates 'the limit exists' from 'the expansion crossed it', so a failure of the previous case can be attributed to the table rather than the counter.

THE PINNED-TABLE BOUNDARY, accepting half. VERIFIED by reading the emitted requestedLanguageRanges: sixteen header entries expand to exactly 32 parsed ranges — the documented MAXIMUM_LANGUAGE_RANGES (LocaleMatcher.java:52) — and the request succeeds, selecting fr. The count is only reproducible against the pinned equivalence table, so a port whose table differs by a single entry lands on the wrong side of the boundary.

thrown.message: range=

cases.notes: A whitespace-only header. INFORMATIONAL: the JDK parser throws rather than producing an empty list — contrast shape.empty-range-list-yields-no-match, which reaches the library with a genuinely empty list and returns NONE. The two rows together show that 'blank header' and 'empty range list' are different inputs, which is the distinction bestMatchForAcceptLanguage collapses and matchFor does not. CROSS-REFERENCE: accept-language.blank.whitespace-only states the same input as REQUIRED portable behavior through bestMatchForAcceptLanguage, where it returns the configured fallback rather than throwing. The row stays informational because THIS operation hands the header to LanguageRange.parse before the library is reached.

thrown.message: range=

cases.notes: An empty HTTP list element between two valid ranges — the exact shape LocaleMatcher.normalizeAcceptLanguage exists to strip before parsing (LocaleMatcher.java:143-160). INFORMATIONAL: the throw is the JDK parser's, raised in the harness before the library, and the library's own normalizing entry point is unreachable from the corpus. CROSS-REFERENCE: this header is not malformed to Lokalized at all -- empty HTTP list elements are exactly what LocaleMatcher.normalizeAcceptLanguage exists to remove. accept-language.empty-element.interior states the same input as REQUIRED portable behavior through bestMatchForAcceptLanguage, where it answers fr instead of throwing. The row stays informational because THIS operation hands the header to LanguageRange.parse before the library is reached.

thrown.message: range=notaheader!

cases.notes: Free text that is not a language range at all. INFORMATIONAL: the corpus's string form of languageRanges is parsed by java.util.Locale.LanguageRange.parse inside the oracle harness (VectorOracle.java:577) before the library is reached, so the recorded throw carries the JDK parser's identity and message rather than Lokalized's. A JS port is not expected to reproduce that text; the row documents which header shapes never reach the matcher at all. Lokalized's own fail-soft entry point, LocaleMatcher.bestMatchForAcceptLanguage, would return the fallback for this instead of throwing, and is not reachable through any corpus operation.

thrown.message: range=	fr

cases.notes: RFC 9110 permits horizontal tab as optional whitespace and the JDK parser rejects it — again the shape LocaleMatcher.normalizeAcceptLanguage converts before parsing. INFORMATIONAL: the throw is raised in the harness before the library. Attributable because the space-form control below, identical but for the tab, parses and negotiates. CROSS-REFERENCE: accept-language.ows.leading-tab states the same input as REQUIRED portable behavior through bestMatchForAcceptLanguage, where the tab is trimmed as RFC 9110 optional whitespace and the answer is fr, not a throw. The row stays informational because THIS operation hands the header to LanguageRange.parse before the library is reached.

thrown.message: weight="abc" for language range "fr"

cases.notes: A well-formed range with a non-numeric q value. INFORMATIONAL for the same reason as its neighbours: the throw comes from the JDK parser in the harness, before the library. Recorded so a port knows this shape is a parse-time rejection rather than a match-time one.

The POSITIVE control for the whitespace rows, and PORTABLE rather than informational: this one does not throw. MEASURED — leading optional whitespace and whitespace after the comma parse cleanly and the higher-weighted later entry is selected at its own weight, so the tab row above is about the tab specifically and not about optional whitespace in general. A port whose header parser trims aggressively enough to accept the tab fails the pair by passing both.

thrown.message: weight=1.5 for language range "fr". It must be between 0.0 and 1.0.

cases.notes: A q value above the RFC-permitted maximum. INFORMATIONAL: rejected by the JDK parser in the harness before the library is reached.

The control that makes the row above legible: a regional range with no loaded regional source reaches the bare language through CLDR parent fallback, reported with the fallback match type and the caller's own range at its stated weight. Also the only place in this flat fixture where a non-exact match type is produced at all.
The mirror: excluding the other regional source moves the answer back. Together the two prove the exclusion is targeted at the named range rather than a fixed reordering.

Rejecting the only positive language leaves nothing: no match at all, NOT the configured fallback. matchFor is the strict entry point and must not manufacture a fallback match (LocaleMatcher.java:47-52); bestMatchFor is the one that substitutes the fallback, and no corpus operation reaches it.

The same exclusion against an extended range instead of a bare one: compare tiebreaker.en-star-first-order, which is this request minus the exclusion and selects the other source. Contrast chooser.equal-specificity-exclusion-is-inert, where the excluded range is NOT more specific than the wildcard range and therefore does nothing. The two rows together define when an exclusion fires.

THE SHARPEST q=0 CASE. Compare tiebreaker.en-bare-first-order, whose request is this one minus the exclusion: adding en-US;q=0 to a header whose only positive range is en;q=1 moves the answer to the other regional source. Java's own comment at DefaultStrings.java:1717-1722 states exactly this. The exclusion bites because en-US;q=0 is an EXACT depth-2 cell while the positive bare en is only a heuristic one; a port that applied q=0 only to ranges matching a locale exactly, or that let the broad positive range reach back over the excluded one, still answers en-US.
Every preference rejected: still no match. Pins that the all-zero path is the same NONE as the nothing-matched path rather than an error, which a port could plausibly get wrong in either direction.
A header consisting of a single q=0 range yields NO match even though that language is loaded and no other preference competes for it, and specifically not the fallback.
A q=0 on a language that is not loaded must be inert rather than poisoning the whole request. Contrast rejection.sole-zero-weight-yields-no-match, whose q=0 names a loaded language.

THE CASE THAT SEPARATES REJECTION FROM RANKING. Compare rejection.derived-range-without-exclusion-control, which is this request minus the fr;q=0 and DOES select fr through CLDR fallback at 0.9. Here the exact-tag exclusion is more specific than the higher-weighted derived range that reaches the same locale, so it governs and the whole request yields no match. A port that ranked by weight — 0.9 beats 0.0 — selects fr. A port that applied q=0 only when nothing else matched also selects fr.

The section 8.3 clause 'advances to a later matching preference BEFORE fallback' asserted end to end rather than only in the diagnostic channel. The unmatched leading preference is skipped, the second serves the translation, and attemptedLocales plus the result's fallback flag show the configured fallback was never consulted. A port that fell back to the instance locale on a first-preference miss and then recovered would produce the same translation but a different attempted-locale chain.
The same header shape with the language groups swapped, so the previous row's result cannot be an artifact of en being the configured fallback.

A real Chrome-shaped header, and a genuine choice between two live cells rather than an artifact. MEASURED SEPARATELY: en-US alone DOES reach the loaded en, through CLDR fallback, at weight 1. Yet here the answer is en reported as EXACT at 0.9, because a locale's effective quality comes from its MOST SPECIFIC matching range (DefaultStrings.java:1717-1722, LocaleMatcher.java:55-58), not its highest-weighted one. A port taking the maximum weight of any matching range reports 1 and the wrong languageRange and matchType while still selecting the right locale.

The same range appears twice at different weights. MEASURED: the parsed list collapses to ONE entry keeping the FIRST occurrence's weight, so the emitted requestedLanguageRanges has a single member and the reported effectiveWeight is the lower 0.5, not the later 0.9. A port whose header parser deduplicated to the maximum weight, or kept both entries, differs in both channels.

An empty parsed range list is a distinct early-return path (DefaultStrings.java:1558) from a list that matches nothing. Emits an empty requestedLanguageRanges alongside NONE, which is how a port proves it did not substitute the fallback or the instance locale. Reached through the explicit array form, since no header string parses to an empty list.

Equal EXPLICIT weights rather than equal implicit ones, and at a weight below 1, so the rule is shown not to depend on the q=1 default. The reported effectiveWeight is the shared 0.5, not a normalized 1.

Two ranges at the implicit q=1. Java sorts by weight descending only (DefaultStrings.java:1562, a stable sort), so equal weights leave list order intact and the first entry wins. This pins the tiebreak that the weight rule alone does not determine.

The same two languages in the opposite order. The answer must flip. A port using an unstable sort, or one that broke weight ties by locale tag or by supported-locale order, returns the same language for both halves.

MOVED TO matchFor DELIBERATELY? No — this row keeps its per-call header on getResult in the paired row below; here it stays a matcher observation of the same header shape used by ingress-smoke's supplied-match fixture, so the whole-list solver's answer for that header is pinned independently of any resolution behavior.
Three-way equal weight: the first listed wins, which rules out 'ties go to the supported-locale order' (de sorts first among the loaded set) and 'ties go to the fallback' (en is the fallback).

The advance-past-unmatched clause taken two steps rather than the one ingress-smoke pins: the two highest-weighted preferences match nothing, the third does, and the fourth is never reached. The reported effectiveWeight is the third entry's q, which is how a port proves it advanced rather than restarted or normalized.

Weight beats list position with three competing preferences, not just two: the middle entry carries the highest q and wins, and the reported effectiveWeight is its q rather than 1. ingress-smoke pins the two-entry version; a port that sorted stably but compared only adjacent pairs could pass that and fail this.
The single-locale kernel counterpart, asserting the two solvers agree on a tiebreaker-decided answer and not merely on exact matches.

The same file, same package, named explicitly instead of discovered. loadFromClasspathResources validates the locale key and the resource PATH but never the filename, so the bytes load cleanly under the caller's key with no warning. A port that runs its filename validator on explicit resource paths rejects a file the reference implementation accepts.

Filename 'en.GB' — a dot where a hyphen belongs, no extension. A port that accepted dot as a subtag separator would load an 'en-GB' that does not exist; one that treated '.GB' as an extension would derive 'en', collide with the real en file, and hard-fail.
The filesystem half of the dotted-stem pair.
A nine-letter extensionless stem, one past the pattern's 8-character subtag ceiling. Skipped in silence — the control for the nine-letter .json case, which throws on the identical stem.
The filesystem half of the over-long-stem pair.

Filename 'de.txt' — a VALID tag under the wrong extension. Only .json is stripped, so the full name is tested against the tag pattern and the dot defeats it: skipped, with no warning. A port that strips whatever follows the last dot loads a spurious 'de' locale here.
The filesystem half. The two paths agree because the name returns null rather than throwing — that agreement is what separates this shape from the .json shapes.

Filename 'de.' — a valid tag with a bare trailing dot. Neither the .json branch nor the tag pattern accepts it, so it is skipped in silence. A port that trims trailing dots before matching loads a locale the reference implementation does not.
The filesystem half of the trailing-dot pair.

Filename 'i-klingon.json'. MEASURED: it loads, and the locale key is 'tlh' — the filename's own tag never appears in the loaded set. Filename 'de-de.json'. The filename's spelling is accepted but the emitted locale key comes from Locale.forLanguageTag, not from the filename: the region is upper-cased. A port that keys its catalog map by the raw stem produces a different key and every later lookup misses.
The filesystem half of the region-canonicalisation pair.

Filename 'zh-hant.json'. Script subtags canonicalise to Title case where regions canonicalise to UPPER, so this is a different transform from the de-de case and a port that hardcodes one rule for 'everything after the language' emits 'zh-HANT' here.
The filesystem half of the script-canonicalisation pair.

Filename 'x-custom.json'. isLanguageTag returns true for an 'x-' stem before it ever consults CLDR, so a private-use tag is loadable from a filename. A port that requires a known language rejects this and converts a working catalog into a warning.
The filesystem half of the private-use pair. A port that rejected the stem here would hard-fail the whole directory rather than merely losing one file.

Filename 'deu.json' — the alpha-3 code for a language that also has an alpha-2 code. MEASURED: the key stays 'deu' and is NOT folded to 'de'. Paired with the legacy-tag case this draws the line between the rewriting Java does and the rewriting it does not.
The filesystem half of the alpha-3 pair.

The filesystem half of the undetermined-tag pair.

A port that implements the exception as an equality test against 'und' turns a loadable catalog into a warning here while passing the plain-'und' case.

Filename 'X-Custom.json'. The 'x-' escape hatch lowercases with Locale.ROOT before testing the prefix, so an uppercase marker takes it too, and the key canonicalises to lowercase. A port testing a raw 'x-' prefix falls through to the CLDR lookup and loses this catalog; one that keeps the filename's case emits 'X-Custom'.
The filesystem half of the uppercase private-use pair.

A valid tag WITH the .json extension, which classpath-smoke never wrote — every fixture there used extensionless names. A port that never strips an extension, or that treats any dot as disqualifying, loads one locale here instead of two.
The filesystem half. Both paths share languageTagForFileName, so this pins that the .json extension is accepted identically on both and that no warning appears on either.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale 'und' found at 'classpath-resources-catalog/en' and 'classpath-resources-catalog/de'

cases.notes: MEASURED: with a collision at entries 1-2 and a shape-invalid path at entry 3, the DUPLICATE exception wins, not the IllegalArgumentException. Validation and conflict detection are interleaved per entry in a single mapping-order pass, so a port that ran all path validation first and then looked for duplicates throws the wrong exception type. Its mirror is path.validation-precedes-any-load, where the invalid path is reached first.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale 'und' found at 'classpath-resources-catalog/en' and 'classpath-resources-catalog/de'

cases.notes: THE 8.3 CLAUSE ITSELF, and the correction to the authored set, which filed this diagnostic as unreachable. It is reachable. MEASURED: Locale.forLanguageTag("und") has language "" while Locale.forLanguageTag("UND") has language "und" — the JDK's getInstance(LanguageTag) compares the RAW-CASE subtag against "und" before lowercasing, so the two Locales are NOT equal yet both render toLanguageTag() == "und". They therefore survive as two LinkedHashMap entries, reach putIfAbsent on the rendered tag, and produce 'Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale \'und\' found at \'classpath-resources-catalog/en\' and \'classpath-resources-catalog/de\'' — a LocalizedStringLoadingException naming BOTH resource paths (:678-681). A port keying by raw string loads two locales; one keying by canonical tag with last-wins loads one.

load.failureMessage: Classpath resource mapping contains 3 localized strings files, exceeding the aggregate localized strings file limit of 2

cases.notes: MEASURED: an over-limit map that also collides reports the FILE-COUNT failure, because the count is taken from resourcePathByLocale.size() before the entry loop begins — and note the size counts the two colliding keys separately, so the reported count is 3. Completes the precedence chain: map-size count, then per-entry locale validation, path validation and conflict detection in mapping order, then the tag-sorted load loop.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale 'und' found at 'classpath-resources-catalog/en' and 'classpath-resources-catalog/en'

cases.notes: MEASURED: both keys pointing at the SAME path still throws, naming that one path twice. The check is on the rendered locale tag alone; identical values are not forgiven. Read against multi.same-resource-under-two-keys — where one resource under two DIFFERENT tags loads twice without complaint — this fixes the conflict predicate precisely as tag collision, never path collision.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale 'und' found at 'classpath-resources-catalog/de' and 'classpath-resources-catalog/en'

cases.notes: MEASURED: the same two entries with the mapping order exchanged names the two sources in the OPPOSITE order — 'found at ...de and ...en'. The first-named source is the incumbent from putIfAbsent, i.e. mapping order, NOT rendered-tag order and not path order. Half of a two-case assertion with the case above; without it a port could pass by sorting the two paths.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings resource mapping for locale 'und-Latn' found at 'classpath-resources-catalog/en' and 'classpath-resources-catalog/de'

cases.notes: MEASURED: the same collision with a script subtag attached — 'Duplicate ... for locale \'und-Latn\' found at ... and ...'. Pins that the quirk lives in the case of the und LANGUAGE subtag, not in the whole tag being literally "und", so a port cannot paper over the conflict clause by special-casing one string. Note the contrast with und-Latn/und-latn, which ARE equal Locales and collapse silently.

The control that makes the conflict cases interpretable. MEASURED: 'UND' on its own passes validateExplicitLocale and loads cleanly under tag 'und' with Only.En. So the exception above is a genuine collision between two accepted keys, not a rejection of the uppercase spelling — a distinction a port will otherwise get wrong by rejecting 'UND' outright and passing the conflict cases for the wrong reason.

load.failureMessage: classpath:classpath-resources-malformed/blank: a localized strings file may not be blank; use an empty JSON object ({}) for an empty file

cases.notes: MEASURED: a zero-byte resource is a distinct rejection from a parse error — 'a localized strings file may not be blank; use an empty JSON object ({}) for an empty file', with no line:column. Pins WHICH failure a port must produce for emptiness rather than letting it fall through to the JSON parser.

warnings.message: Ignoring classpath resource '<fixtures>/classpath-resources-malformed/broken.json': File 'broken.json' ends with .json but is not named with a valid IETF BCP 47 language tag. Use names like 'en', 'en.json', or 'en-US.json'

cases.notes: The discovery control for the case above, on the identical directory. MEASURED: discovery loads ONLY en; it skips 'messages', 'blank' and 'dupes' SILENTLY — never opening them, so their content failures (zero bytes, duplicate member) are invisible — and warns INVALID_CLASSPATH_LOCALE_FILENAME for 'broken.json'. Distinct-but-equivalent loaded tags must remain SEPARATE catalogs: the load reports en, hy-AM and hy-SU with different key sets. A port that canonicalizes filenames before keying (hy-SU to hy-AM) merges them and loses a key set here; a port that treats them as a conflict fails the load outright.

The clause's named mo/ro pair at the LOADER boundary: two files whose tags are canonically equivalent must load as two locales, mo and ro, each keeping its own keys. A port that canonicalizes the filename before keying reports one locale here. Load-only because the corresponding Strings instance is not constructible without tiebreakers this repository's ingest tool cannot express (see skipped).

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Pair.InBoth' for locale 'hy'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [hy]

cases.notes: Truncation on a candidate that has NO catalog: the deduped chain for bare hy starts with hy itself, which is not loaded and is therefore recorded verbatim (DefaultStrings.java:2495), so neverFallback stops there and returns the key even though the very next candidate would have translated. A port that omits catalog-less candidates from the chain resolves this in hy-AM instead.

Tiebreaker order must not override exact identity: with hy-SU listed first, an explicit hy-AM request still resolves in hy-AM with a one-entry attempted list. A port that consults tiebreakers before checking the exact catalog map fails here while passing every other case in this fixture.

The configured fallback locale arm-SU is equivalent to two loaded catalogs at once, so construction resolves it through the tiebreaker list (DefaultStrings.java:452-465) and adopts hy-AM. Every unrelated request therefore ends at hy-AM, and match.fallbackLocale reports hy-AM rather than the configured arm-SU. Paired with its su-first twin.

Same files, same configured fallback tag, reversed tiebreaker list: the effective fallback locale must flip to hy-SU, changing both the tail of the attempted chain and the fallbackLocale carried in every match object. A port that resolves an ambiguous fallback by sorting, or by first-loaded, produces the am-first answer for both fixtures.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'FallbackAlias.OnlyInEn' for locale 'fr'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [fr, ro]

cases.notes: Proof that the resolved fallback really is ro and not en: a key that exists only in the en catalog is unreachable from an unrelated request and the key is returned. Guards against a port that quietly treats every loaded locale as a terminal fallback.

The control that keeps the previous case honest: en is not dead, merely not the fallback. Requesting en resolves the same key in one attempt with match type EXACT, while match.fallbackLocale still reports ro.
Requesting the configured-but-unloaded fallback tag itself: candidate resolution and fallback resolution must agree on ro, and the whole chain dedups to a single entry.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'FallbackAlias.Missing' for locale 'fr'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [fr, ro]

cases.notes: The configured fallback locale is itself resolved through equivalence at construction (DefaultStrings.java:448-449): fallbackLocale mo becomes ro because ro is the only canonically-equivalent loaded locale. An unrelated request therefore attempts [fr, ro] and the emitted match.fallbackLocale is ro. A port that stores the configured tag verbatim attempts mo, finds nothing, and reports a fallbackLocale of mo in every match object it ever emits.

The file named iw is keyed by Locale.forLanguageTag('iw'), whose language tag is he (LocalizedStringLoader.java:1260-1269), so the loaded locale set is [en, he] and the keys sit under he. A port that keys catalogs by the literal filename reports iw and then silently misses every he request.
The modern spelling must produce an observation identical to the iw request, including match type EXACT. The pair pins that he and iw are one locale here, in contrast with hy-AM/hy-SU, which are two.

Requesting the superseded spelling reaches the catalog and reports resolvedLocale he, not iw - the requested tag is normalized by Locale identity before the walk starts, unlike mo and hy-SU which stay distinct Locale values and are resolved by CLDR equivalence instead.

Same fixture, same key, per-call fallbackOnAnyFailure: the walk continues past the throwing ro catalog and resolves in en with status TRANSLATED and no failure recorded. Paired with the default-policy sibling this proves the shorter list came from the POLICY, while the pair against the ro-request control proves the list's contents came from DEDUP.
