failureCause.message: Unable to resolve generated placeholder 'itemWord' (LanguageFormTranslation) for key 'Dedup.ResolutionFailure'; definition declared at Dedup.ResolutionFailure: Missing value for placeholder 'absentCount' in key 'Dedup.ResolutionFailure'

cases.notes: The ro catalog's cardinality placeholder reads a context name the call does not supply and throws (DefaultStrings.java:966-968); the default policy, fallbackOnMissingTranslationOrNoMatchingAlternative, refuses to continue on RESOLUTION_FAILURE, so attemptedLocales truncates to the deduped ro and the plain en text one candidate later is forfeited. Pins the failure reason, the cause type and the truncated list together, and the fixture's ro catalog is otherwise warning-clean so this is the only defect in play.

The key exists in both catalogs. First-wins dedup keeps the ro entry at position 0, so ro's text wins and attemptedLocales never reaches en. A port that deduped last-wins, or that ordered the fallback locale first, returns en's text.

Control for every mo case in this family: the directory loads exactly [en, ro] with those key sets and NO warnings. No mo catalog exists, so any mo observation below is candidate-walk behavior and not loading behavior. A port whose loader invented a mo catalog would show it here instead of failing the resolution cases mysteriously.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.Missing' for locale 'mo'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro, en]

cases.notes: The same collapse observed through the failure channel: the handler's attemptedLocales must be the deduped [ro, en], identical to the result's, and the failure reason must be MISSING_TRANSLATION rather than anything the extra duplicate attempt would have produced.

First-wins dedup shortens the list: raw candidates [mo, ro, en] collapse to two because mo and ro resolve to the same loaded catalog (putIfAbsent, DefaultStrings.java:2498). The key resolves in the fallback, so isFallback and resolvedLocale are pinned too. A non-deduping port reports three attempted locales for a translation that is otherwise identical.

The ordering trap. fallbackLocalesFor(mo-MD) is [mo-MD, mo, ro-MD, ro] (verified); only mo resolves onto loaded ro, ro-MD resolves to nothing and is recorded as itself, and the later raw ro is dropped as a duplicate. attemptedLocales must be [mo-MD, ro, ro-MD, en] - ro occupies mo's SLOT and therefore precedes ro-MD. A port that dedups after the walk, or that sorts candidates, or that resolves aliases lazily, gets this order wrong even when it gets the set right.

cases.notes: Flagship policy-truncation-through-dedup case: the resolution failure fires at chain position 2, which is ro only because dedup moved it there, so the default policy truncates attemptedLocales to [mo-MD, ro]. A port that records the requested tag instead of the resolved one, or that keeps both, truncates at a different locale or a different length with the same failure reason.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.OnlyInEn' for locale 'mo'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro]

cases.notes: Truncation with a visible cost: the key exists in en and is one candidate away, but neverFallback halts at the deduped ro, so the status is RETURNED_KEY. Pairs with dedup-and-candidates.moro.mo-chain-dedups-to-two-entries, which resolves the same key under the default policy.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.Missing' for locale 'mo'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro]

cases.notes: Policy truncation whose CONTENT is decided by dedup: neverFallback stops after the first distinct candidate, and that candidate is ro, not the requested mo. A port that stops after the first raw candidate produces a list of the same length with the wrong locale in it - length alone would not catch this, which is why the case asserts the whole list.

The clause's named case. DefaultStrings.java:2493-2499 resolves each raw candidate through localizedStringsFor BEFORE recording it, so the attempted locale for mo is the loaded ro and attemptedLocales is exactly one entry long. A port that pushes the requested tag and only later maps it to a catalog emits ["mo"] here; a port that records both emits ["mo","ro"].

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.Missing' for locale 'ro'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro, en]

cases.notes: Control: requesting the loaded tag directly must yield the SAME attempted list as requesting mo, differing only in the diagnostic channel (match type EXACT here versus CANONICAL for mo). Proves the two requests converge after dedup rather than mo being special-cased, and keeps the two channels distinguishable.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.Missing' for locale 'mo'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro]

cases.notes: Every raw candidate for mo collapses onto the single loaded ro, so the walk has exactly ONE candidate: attemptedLocales is [ro] even though the default policy would happily continue. A port that dedups the attempted list only for display would call the policy twice more and emit [ro, ro, ro].

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Dedup.Missing' for locale 'mo'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ro]

cases.notes: No policy call after the final distinct candidate, made observable: DefaultStrings.java:731 breaks before the policy call on line 734 when the candidate is last, so neverFallback must produce an observation IDENTICAL to its default-policy sibling above. The oracle has no policy-invocation counter, so this identity pair is the strongest available lock - and it does discriminate, because a port that dedups late emits [ro, ro, ro] under the default policy and [ro] under never.

Success control for the single-distinct-candidate fixture: the one deduped candidate is also the fallback locale, resolvedLocale is ro, attemptedLocales has one entry, and isFallback is pinned for the case where the resolved locale and the fallback locale coincide.

Control for the previous case: the same entry resolved directly, with no fallback, must isolate identically. Establishes that the isolation seen on the English request comes from the donor locale rather than from something specific to the fallback path. This case alone does not discriminate; it exists to attribute the sibling's result.

The single most decisive case in the family: CARDINALITY_ZERO can only be produced by Arabic rules, and here Arabic is the donor for an English request. Any implementation that evaluates under the requested locale is structurally incapable of emitting this branch.
11 is MANY under ar (n%100 = 11..99) and OTHER under en. Completes en->ar coverage across all four of Arabic's non-catch-all categories.

CARDINALITY_TWO is likewise unreachable from any other locale in this family. Pairs with the ZERO case so the en->ar direction is proved by two categories rather than one, guarding against a port that special-cases zero.
3 is FEW under the Arabic donor (n%100 = 3..10) and OTHER under en. Covers a mainstream Arabic category, so a port cannot pass the en->ar direction by hard-coding zero and two.

Bidi isolation of a caller-supplied value is decided by shouldApplyBidiIsolation(locale, bidiIsolation) inside interpolateTemplate, where `locale` is the same donor locale used for plural selection. With the default BidiIsolation.RTL_LOCALES an English request served by the Arabic donor must therefore still be isolated -- confirmed against the oracle, which emits U+2068 Sarah U+2069. Without this case a port would key isolation off the requested locale and silently drop the isolate marks that keep a Latin name from reordering inside Arabic text.
French requests, Arabic supplies: zero is ONE in fr and ZERO in ar. A wrong answer here produces a grammatical singular for an empty count in an RTL catalog.
11 is OTHER in fr and MANY in ar. Third fr->ar count, so the pair is discriminated across three different Arabic categories.
2 is OTHER in fr and TWO in ar. Covers the fr->ar pair on Arabic's dual category, which French does not have at all.
Polish requests, Arabic supplies: zero is MANY in pl and ZERO in ar. Both languages have rich category sets, so this pair is not covered by the English cases.
2 is FEW in pl and TWO in ar -- two different specific categories. This is the shape that catches a port implementing 'prefer the more specific category across both locales'.

200 is OTHER in ar (n%100 = 0) and MANY in pl -- the direction where the REQUESTING locale has the more specific category. Without this direction the pl->ar pair could be passed by a specificity-biased port.
Russian requests, Arabic supplies: zero is MANY in ru and ZERO in ar. Distinct from pl->ar because pl and ru reach MANY at zero through different rule limbs.
2 is FEW in ru and TWO in ar. Specific-versus-specific across the ru->ar pair.
200 is MANY in ru and OTHER in ar. Completes the ru->ar direction at a count where the donor lands on its catch-all.
21 is ONE in ru and MANY in ar -- singular/plural polarity inverted between requester and donor. A port evaluating under the requested locale would serve an Arabic singular for twenty-one items.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell.Named {{name}}' for locale 'ar'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ar, en]

cases.notes: The asymmetry that makes the donor rule worth stating precisely. This key exists in no catalog, so the default returnKey handler interpolates the key itself -- and interpolateFailureKey is handed the REQUESTED locale, because there is no donor. Confirmed against the oracle: the Arabic request yields 'Farewell.Named ⁨Sarah⁩' (isolated) while the sibling resolved case, which had an English donor, is not isolated. Without this case a port would plausibly unify the two paths on one locale and be wrong on exactly one of them.

The killer bidi case. Arabic is requested, the English donor supplies, and because the RTL_LOCALES policy is evaluated against the DONOR locale the caller-supplied value is NOT isolated even though the request was for an RTL locale -- confirmed against the oracle, which emits a bare 'Hello, Sarah'. A JS port that keys isolation off the requested locale emits stray U+2068/U+2069 around every value in this situation, which is invisible in most assertions and corrupts exact string comparisons downstream.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Farewell.Named {{name}}' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: Control for the returned-key path: the same missing key requested under English must not isolate. Together with the Arabic returned-key case this pins the two-rule picture -- donor locale for resolved entries, requested locale for returned keys.

Control for the previous case: the same entry resolved directly under English must also be un-isolated, so the absence of isolate marks in the Arabic request is attributable to the donor locale rather than to isolation being off everywhere. Does not discriminate on its own.

Control: requesting English resolves in the English catalog with no Polish candidate involved, and 2 is OTHER so the OTHER-gated alternative matches. Establishes what the en entry does on its own, so the pass-through cases can be attributed to the chain.

1 is ONE under both pl and en, so neither candidate's alternative matches and the en entry's default translation is used. CORRECTION applied during review: this case does NOT discriminate on evaluation locale, and the authored note implied it did. Its real proposition is that NO_MATCHING_ALTERNATIVE really does continue the chain -- a port that stopped at the first candidate would return the key instead of en:default.

2 is FEW under Polish, so the pl entry's alternative matches and resolution stops at the first candidate with resolvedLocale pl. CORRECTION applied during review: the authored note claimed this discriminates a requested-locale port. It does not -- the requester and the first donor are the same locale here, so both behave identically. What it actually catches is a port that evaluates every candidate under the FALLBACK locale, which would classify 2 as OTHER, fall through to the en entry, and return en:OTHER-branch with resolvedLocale en.

Same two-locale traversal at a count where Polish says MANY through a different rule limb (i%10 = 1 and i != 1) and English says OTHER, so the pass-through and the second evaluation are exercised again on different rule machinery. Guards against a port that re-evaluates under the second donor but caches the first donor's classification of the number.

The discriminating case in this fixture. 5 is MANY in pl so the first candidate's FEW-gated alternative does not match and, having no default translation, yields NO_MATCHING_ALTERNATIVE and the chain continues. The en candidate then classifies the same 5 as OTHER under ENGLISH rules and matches its OTHER-gated alternative (oracle: 'en:OTHER-branch', resolvedLocale en). A port that reused the requested locale (pl) for the second candidate would classify 5 as MANY there too, match nothing, and fall to the en entry's default translation instead.
Arabic requests, English supplies: zero must select the English OTHER branch. A port evaluating under Arabic would look for CARDINALITY_ZERO, which this realistic English catalog does not declare.
Same detector on Arabic's dual category, which an English catalog can never satisfy.
Third Arabic count against the English donor, this time on Arabic's few-rule. Three counts across three Arabic categories make an accidental pass implausible.
Arabic also has exactly one ordinal category and is RTL, so this checks the ordinal donor path for a requester differing from the donor in both category count and script direction.

French requests, English supplies: zero must select OTHER, not the ONE branch French rules would choose. Both branches exist in the English catalog, so a wrong port succeeds with different text rather than failing -- the silent-divergence shape.

Polish requests, an English catalog declaring only ONE and OTHER supplies. Under English rules 2 is OTHER and resolution succeeds; a port evaluating under Polish selects FEW, finds no branch, and takes the missing-branch failure path. Correct behavior succeeds and wrong behavior fails loudly -- and this is the realistic configuration, because real English catalogs do not carry Slavic branches.
Same detector at a count that maps to Polish MANY rather than FEW, so a port that happened to declare a FEW widening but not a MANY one is still caught.
Portuguese requests, English supplies: zero is ONE in pt and OTHER in en, and both branches exist, so this is a silent-divergence detector for the pt->en direction.
Russian requests, English supplies. This is the single most common real-world fallback in a shipped application, so its regression would be the widest.

21 is ONE in ru and OTHER in en. Unlike the FEW and MANY cases this one does NOT fail under wrong evaluation -- it silently emits the singular branch. That makes it the case that catches a port whose only defense against wrong-locale evaluation is that a missing branch happens to throw.
Second Russian count against the English donor, mapping to ru's many-rule rather than its few-rule.
2 is ORDINALITY_TWO in en. Second English ordinal category through a Russian request, so a port cannot pass by implementing only the ordinal few-rule.
21 is ORDINALITY_ONE in en (n%10 = 1 and n%100 != 11). Proves the donor's full ordinal rule including its modulus limbs runs, not a truncated 1/2/3 lookup table.

The ordinality mirror of the ru-donor ordinal cases: here the donor is the language WITH ordinal categories and the requester is the one without. 3 is ORDINALITY_FEW in en and ORDINALITY_OTHER in ru, and both branches exist, so a port evaluating under the requester silently degrades every ordinal served by an English fallback to the catch-all form.
Arabic requests, French supplies: zero is ZERO in ar and ONE in fr. Mirror of fr->ar in the ar-donor fixture.
2 is TWO in ar and OTHER in fr. Second ar->fr count on Arabic's dual category.
3 is FEW in ar and OTHER in fr. Third ar->fr count, covering Arabic's few-rule under a coarse donor.

English requests, French supplies: zero is ONE in fr and OTHER in en. The en/fr pair is the one a port author is most likely to assume equivalent, since both have small category sets -- but they disagree at zero, the count a fallback is most likely to be exercised with.

One million is MANY in fr (e = 0 and i != 0 and i%1000000 = 0 and v = 0) and OTHER in en. English has no MANY category at all, so this proves the donor's full rule runs rather than a reduced version derived from the requester.

Tagged decimal so the visible decimal place reaches Java intact. 1.5 is ONE in fr because its rule tests i = 0,1 and ignores v, but OTHER in en because en's rule requires v = 0. Catches a port that evaluates the integer operand under the donor while applying the requester's v-guard.
Polish requests, French supplies. French's one-rule is the broadest in the family, so zero must select ONE where Polish would say MANY. Mirror of fr->pl in the pl-donor fixture.
2 is OTHER in fr and FEW in pl -- here the DONOR has the coarser category set. A port biased toward the richer of the two rule sets would pick FEW and be wrong.
Russian requests, French supplies: zero is MANY in ru and ONE in fr.
2 is FEW in ru and OTHER in fr. Second ru->fr count, on the coarse-donor side.

21 is ONE in ru and OTHER in fr: the requester would produce a singular where the donor produces a plural. Inverts the polarity of the count-0 case in the same pair, so a port cannot pass both with a single directional bias.
Arabic requests, Polish supplies: zero must select Polish MANY, not Arabic ZERO. The ZERO category is unreachable from Polish rules at any count, so a wrong answer here is unambiguous.

100 is OTHER in ar (n%100 = 0) and MANY in pl -- the direction where the DONOR has the more specific category. Without a case in this direction, a port that always preferred whichever locale had the more specific category would still pass the ZERO and TWO cases.
2 is TWO in ar and FEW in pl. Second exotic-category guard for the ar->pl direction, and specific-versus-specific rather than specific-versus-catch-all.

Zero is MANY in pl (v=0 and i!=1 and i%10=0..1) and OTHER in en. Zero is the count implementations most often special-case outside the rule engine, so pinning it on a fallback path is worth its own case.
English requests, Polish supplies: 2 is FEW in pl and OTHER in en. Covers the en->pl pair, which the ru-donor fixture cannot since a fixture has one fallback donor.
5 is MANY in pl, OTHER in en. Together with the count-2 case this proves the en->pl direction distinguishes the donor's FEW and MANY, not merely 'not OTHER'.
French requests, Polish supplies: zero is ONE in fr and MANY in pl -- the count where the two disagree most sharply.
2 is OTHER in fr and FEW in pl. Second fr->pl count so the pair is covered on both sides of the French one/other boundary.

A fractional count carried as a tagged decimal so the visible decimal place reaches Java as BigDecimal rather than being flattened by JSON's single number type. 1.5 is OTHER in pl because every pl rule requires v = 0, but ONE in fr because fr's rule tests i alone. Without this case a port could evaluate the v operand under the requested locale while evaluating i under the donor and still pass every integer case in the family.
Portuguese requests, Polish supplies: zero is ONE in pt (i = 0..1) and MANY in pl. Gives Portuguese a requester role against a Slavic donor, which the pt-pair fixture cannot provide.
2 is OTHER in pt and FEW in pl. Second pt->pl count, so the pair is discriminated on both sides of the Portuguese one/other boundary.
Three-digit instance of the ru->pl divergence, guarding against a port whose Polish many-rule tests only the last two digits.

The reverse of the ru-donor pl-request case: Russian requests, Polish supplies, and 21 is MANY under pl where ru says ONE. Direction matters because a port could hard-code 'Slavic donor wins' in one direction only.
ADDED IN REVIEW. Arabic requests, Portuguese supplies: zero is ONE in pt and ZERO in ar. Uses Arabic's exclusive ZERO category so a wrong answer is unambiguous.
ADDED IN REVIEW. One million is MANY in pt and OTHER in ar (n%100 = 0). The direction where the DONOR has the more specific category, completing the ar->pt pair on both polarities.
ADDED IN REVIEW. 2 is OTHER in pt and TWO in ar. Second exotic-category guard for the ar->pt direction.

ADDED IN REVIEW. English requests, Portuguese supplies: zero is ONE in pt (i = 0..1) and OTHER in en. The plainest en->pt discriminator, and the first case in the corpus where Portuguese is the SUPPLYING locale for a non-Portuguese request -- a role the clause names but the authored set never exercised.
ADDED IN REVIEW. One million is MANY in pt and OTHER in en. English has no MANY category at all, so the branch is only reachable if the donor's rule ran.

ADDED IN REVIEW. Tagged decimal: 1.5 is ONE in pt because i = 1 and pt's rule ignores v, and OTHER in en because en requires v = 0. Same operand distinction as the pt/pt-PT pair, but observed across a language boundary rather than a variant boundary.
ADDED IN REVIEW. Russian requests, Portuguese supplies: zero is ONE in pt and MANY in ru -- singular versus plural, the most visible possible divergence.
ADDED IN REVIEW. 2 is OTHER in pt and FEW in ru: the direction where the REQUESTER has the richer category set. Guards a port biased toward whichever locale is more specific.

Same detector entered from pt-PT, which reaches the English donor after two intermediate candidates (attemptedLocales ['pt-PT','pt','en']) whose catalogs both lack the key. Confirms the number of skipped candidates does not change which locale governs evaluation.

The pt-PT -> pt leg, reached through the CLDR parent chain. Zero is ONE under the pt donor and OTHER under the pt-PT requester. Without this case a port could treat pt-PT as a pure alias of pt -- the shortcut most i18n libraries take -- and never be caught.

Agreement control: 1 is ONE under both pt and pt-PT. Pins that the donor-locale rule does not introduce a difference where the two rule sets genuinely coincide, so a port cannot pass the pair by always choosing the opposite of the requester.

The second and only other place pt and pt-PT disagree: 1.5 is ONE under pt (its rule ignores v) and OTHER under pt-PT (its rule requires v = 0). Tagged as a decimal so the visible decimal place is not erased by JSON. Covers the v-operand half of the divergence, which the count-0 case does not reach.

Three-candidate chain: pt, then pt-PT, then the English fallback locale, with the key present only in the last. Zero is OTHER in en and ONE in pt, so this proves the LAST candidate in a chain is evaluated under its own locale and not under the first one that happened to have a catalog.

One million is MANY in both pt and pt-PT but OTHER in en, and this English catalog declares no MANY branch. Correct behavior resolves; a port evaluating under either Portuguese variant hits the missing-branch path. Asymmetric detector for the three-candidate chain.

The reverse leg: a bare pt request for a key that exists only in pt-PT. pt-PT enters pt's candidate list through the tiebreaker limb of localeFallbackCandidates rather than the parent chain. CORRECTION applied during review: the authored note hedged that the leg might not fire. It does -- the oracle reports attemptedLocales ['pt','pt-PT'] and resolvedLocale pt-PT -- so the case pins BOTH that the tiebreaker limb contributes candidates and that what it contributes is evaluated under its own rules; zero is OTHER under pt-PT and ONE under pt.

Reverse leg on the v-operand divergence: 1.5 is OTHER under pt-PT and ONE under pt. Pairs with the count-0 case so the pt -> pt-PT direction is covered by both of the two counts where the variants disagree.
ADDED IN REVIEW. Arabic requests, pt-PT supplies: zero is OTHER in pt-PT and ZERO in ar.
ADDED IN REVIEW. 2 is OTHER in pt-PT and TWO in ar. Second Arabic exclusive category through a pt-PT donor.

ADDED IN REVIEW. English requests, pt-PT supplies. pt-PT and en agree at every count EXCEPT integer multiples of a million (and compact exponents outside 0..5), where pt-PT says MANY and en says OTHER. This is therefore the only count that can discriminate the en->pt-PT direction at all, and it is the reason pt-PT must not be flattened into en-like two-category handling.

ADDED IN REVIEW. French requests, pt-PT supplies: zero is ONE in fr and OTHER in pt-PT. Pairs with the pt-donor fixture's deliberate omission of French -- fr cannot be discriminated from pt at any value, but it IS discriminated from pt-PT, and this case is where that shows.
ADDED IN REVIEW. Tagged decimal: 1.5 is ONE in fr (rule tests i only) and OTHER in pt-PT (rule requires v = 0). The v-operand half of the fr->pt-PT pair.

ADDED IN REVIEW. Russian requests, pt-PT supplies: zero is OTHER in pt-PT (its one-rule requires i = 1) and MANY in ru. Note this is the OPPOSITE donor answer from the pt-donor fixture's ru@0 case, which is exactly the pt/pt-PT distinction carried into a cross-language fallback.

Paired control for ar-request-count-2: locally resolved Arabic must select TWO. Confirms the port CAN produce TWO, so the fallback case's FEW is a deliberate donor-locale result rather than a missing Arabic rule.

Arabic requests, Russian supplies. ar has a ZERO category (n = 0) and ru does not; 0 must select the Russian MANY branch. The donor catalog declares CARDINALITY_ZERO precisely so a wrong port produces visible wrong text instead of a throw.

100 is OTHER in ar (n%100 = 0 falls through zero/one/two/few/many) and MANY in ru (i%10 = 0). Covers the ar->ru direction at a count where Arabic lands on its catch-all, so a port cannot pass the pair merely by never emitting ZERO or TWO.

2 is TWO in ar (n = 2) and FEW in ru. The TWO category is reachable from no other locale in this family, so this is the sharpest available evidence that the ar->ru direction evaluates under the donor.

Paired control for en-request-count-2: same fixture, same locale, same count, but the key IS in the English catalog so no fallback occurs and English rules legitimately apply. Without this pairing a port that always evaluated under the requested locale would look merely 'different' rather than provably wrong, and one that always evaluated under the fallback locale would go undetected.

The second locale-sensitive channel: a whole-message alternative gated on `itemCount == CARDINALITY_FEW`. ExpressionEvaluator classifies the number under the locale alternativeMatches was handed, which for a fallback entry is the donor. 2 is FEW in ru and OTHER in en, so a port that evaluated alternatives against the requested locale would fall through all three alternatives to the default translation.

21 matches the CARDINALITY_ONE alternative (third in order) under the ru donor but no alternative at all under en, where it is OTHER and would reach the default translation. Distinguishes 'matched a different branch' from 'matched no branch', which are different failure shapes in a port.

Same expression channel at a count that selects the MANY alternative under the donor. The FEW alternative is ordered ahead of it, so this also confirms first-match ordering is decided with the donor's classification.

Three-way discriminator: 0 is MANY under the supplying locale ru (i%10=0), OTHER under the requested locale en, and ONE under this fixture's ambient instanceLocale fr (i = 0,1). Without it, a port that leaked the ambient locale into evaluation would be indistinguishable from one that used the requested locale.

11 exercises ru's `i%100 = 11..14` limb of the many-rule -- the limb that overrides what would otherwise be ONE at i%10=1. en says OTHER. CORRECTION applied during review: the authored note claimed 11 is where ru and pl diverge on MANY membership. It is not. pl reaches MANY at 11 through its own `i != 1 and i%10 = 0..1` limb, so both say MANY; this case's discriminating power is en-versus-ru only.

The English catalog exists but lacks Items.Fallback, so the Russian fallback locale supplies it. 2 is FEW under ru (v=0 and i%10=2..4 and i%100!=12..14) and OTHER under en. A port that classified the count under the requested locale would emit the OTHER branch of a Russian catalog for every English request served by a Slavic donor.
21 is ONE under ru (v=0 and i%10=1 and i%100!=11) -- a category English reserves for exactly 1. Catches a port that 'optimizes' the fallback path by reusing the requested locale's ONE test.

Same donor, a second Russian category: 5 is MANY under ru (i%10=5..9) and OTHER under en. Covers a different limb of ru's many-rule than the count-0 and count-11 cases, so a port with a partially correct rule table cannot pass all three by accident.

Deliberate NEGATIVE pin, and the one case in this family that would NOT change if the donor-locale rule were inverted -- that is exactly its point, and the authored note overclaimed by calling it a discriminator. DefaultStrings selects a gender branch by a direct map lookup on the caller's Gender value with no locale consulted anywhere (verified at DefaultStrings.java:1001-1020), so a fallback must not perturb it. It also confirms the fallback path reaches gender resolution at all. A port that 'improved' gender handling per-locale would otherwise pass the whole corpus.

Second ordinal count on the same donor: 1 is ORDINALITY_ONE in en (n%10=1 and n%100!=11) and ORDINALITY_OTHER in ru. Guards the case where a port special-cases 1 as a universal singular before consulting any locale's ordinal rules.

Ordinality travels the same donor-locale path as cardinality (ordinalityForValue is handed the same `locale` argument). ru has exactly one ordinal category, so the donor entry declares only ORDINALITY_OTHER and resolution succeeds; English would classify 3 as ORDINALITY_FEW and hit the 'Missing Ordinality translation' IllegalStateException. Without this case a port could route cardinality through the donor and ordinality through the requester and still pass every plural case here.

Paired control for fr-request-count-0: locally resolved French must select ONE at zero. Without it a reviewer could not tell whether the fallback case's MANY came from the donor's rules or from a broken French rule table.
French requests, Russian supplies. Zero is ONE in fr (i = 0,1) and MANY in ru. A port that used the requested locale would emit the singular branch of a Russian catalog for a count of zero.
2 is FEW under the ru donor and OTHER under the fr requester. Pairs with the count-0 case so the fr->ru direction is covered on both sides of the French one/other boundary.
5 is MANY under ru and OTHER under fr. Proves the donor's four-way split survives a request from a locale whose only non-catch-all categories are ONE and a millions-only MANY.

Paired control for pl-request-count-21. Resolving locally must give the Polish MANY branch at the same count where the fallback path gives the Russian ONE branch, so the difference is attributable to which catalog supplied the entry and nothing else.

Expression channel across the pl/ru divergence: 21 matches the ONE alternative under the ru donor and would match the MANY alternative under pl. Both branches exist, so this case discriminates purely on which locale drove the comparison -- a port cannot pass it by falling through to the default text.
Second instance of the pl/ru divergence, at three digits, so a port cannot pass the pair by special-casing two-digit numbers. 101 is ONE under ru and MANY under pl.

Polish requests, Russian supplies. Verified against GeneratedCldrPluralData: pl and ru agree at every integer except where i%10=1 and i!=1 and i%100!=11 (21, 31, ..., 101, 1001), where pl says MANY and ru says ONE. This is the only shape that discriminates the pair, so without it the pl->ru direction is untested.

Success control in the same fixture: 1 is ONE under Russian rules and the branch exists, so resolution completes normally. Proves the sibling failures come from the selected category rather than from a broken fixture.

The load-bearing precedence discriminator. VERIFIED: emits 'or-of-and matched'. A port giving '||' and '&&' equal precedence, or binding '||' tighter, would build (alpha||beta)&&gamma = false and emit 'no alternative'. Note the two parses differ in only one direction (alpha||(beta&&gamma) subsumes (alpha||beta)&&gamma), so this shape is the only kind of tuple that can discriminate at all.

cases.notes: STRENGTHENED in review by adding a well-formed sibling placeholder. '2name' fails LocalizedStringUtils.isValidLocalizedStringIdentifier (the pattern is [\p{L}_][\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}_-]*, so a leading digit is rejected), so the lenient path copies the whole '{{2name}}' run through untouched and never consults the context -- the caller's value under that exact name is deliberately NOT substituted. cases.notes: THE MISS CASE, and the highest-value case in this family. The gender-keyed alternatives-only child is selected, both of its nested alternatives miss at packageCount 0, and getInternal returns empty: RETURNED_KEY with failureReason NO_MATCHING_ALTERNATIVE. It must NOT be the later sibling 'packageCount == 0' (which matches this exact context -- see the NEUTER contrast case, which does reach it) and must NOT be the root's own 'Delivery status unavailable.'. cases.notes: Baseline grammatical-case dispatch, selecting the middle of three declared forms. The axis has nine constants and no numeric or CLDR fallback, so the map lookup must be exact. cases.notes: The branch redefines the same placeholder name with a different translation table, so the rendered noun proves whose definition won. A port that let the ancestor definition survive because it was installed first would emit the parent's noun here. Note that this case alone does NOT separate replacement from a per-form merge, because both tables define the same forms and a merge would also let the branch's values win; the partial-branch-table pair below is what settles that.

cases.notes: The branch's replacement table defines only CARDINALITY_OTHER while the parent defines ONE and OTHER, and the value selects ONE. Replacement is whole-definition, so the form is simply absent and resolution fails with 'Missing Cardinality translation for ONE' against a definition declared at 'Partial replacement -> alternative[mode == 1]'. This is the only case in the family that separates replacement from a per-form MERGE: a port that layered the branch table over the parent's would find the parent's 'book' and render successfully.

The live half of the partial-replacement pair: the same branch renders normally for the one form its table does define. Without it the previous case could be passed by a port that rejects the branch outright, or that rejects any table missing a form the locale supports.

Control for whole-definition replacement: with no branch match the parent's table is the only one in scope. It pins that the replacement is scoped to the branch and does not leak upward into the parent's own render.

The positive half of the scope rule: inside an already-expanded generated fragment, a name that is NOT file-defined still resolves from the caller's raw input. A port that treated the nested expansion as a closed scope would report a missing placeholder here.

cases.notes: The expression alternative of a generated fragment references a sibling generated placeholder whose text would satisfy the comparison, and that sibling is resolved first because the template names it first. Java evaluates fragment alternatives against the caller's context only, so the operand is absent and evaluation throws ExpressionEvaluationException 'No value was provided for placeholder size'. A port that evaluated fragment expressions against the generated context would select the alternative and render a match Java never produces.

Same sharpening for a generated fragment's alternative expression: the generated size is "10" and the caller's size is 3, and the alternative tests size == 10. Java evaluates against the caller's 3, so the alternative does not fire, while the template still interpolates the generated "10". A port evaluating fragment expressions against the generated context selects the alternative and renders a different, successful string.

cases.notes: A language-form placeholder whose selector names a SIBLING generated placeholder. The sibling is referenced first in the template, so it is resolved to the text "5" before the language form is reached; Java still resolves selectors against the caller's immutable context only, finds nothing, and fails with 'Missing value for placeholder level'. A port that fed generated values back into selectors would find "5" waiting and render successfully.

The sharp form of the selector-scope rule, on the same key. A generated placeholder named level produces the text "5" while the caller supplies level = 1, and a sibling language form selects on that name. Java reads the caller's 1 (CARDINALITY_ONE) for selection and the generated "5" for interpolation, so all three plausible ports render visibly different strings: reading generated values at selection yields the OTHER form, and preferring raw input at interpolation prints "1" in the leading position.

Both range endpoints supplied by the caller as 1, against a generated minHours of "2". Java's range therefore classifies ONE-to-ONE while the template still renders the generated "2". A port that read the generated "2" as the range start would classify the range differently, and a port that preferred raw input at interpolation would print "1". It also pins that BOTH endpoints are read from the caller, not just the start.

cases.notes: The range form of a language-form placeholder. Both endpoints are read from the caller's context; the caller supplies only the end, so resolution fails with 'Missing range start placeholder minHours' even though a generated placeholder named minHours exists AND has already been resolved to the numeric text "2" because the template references it first. That last part is what makes the case decisive: a port that read range endpoints out of the generated context would find "2" waiting for it and render a translation Java never produces.

The other form of the same-name-both-scopes key. Paired with the plural case it shows the selector really consumes the caller's NUMBER rather than a fixed value, which a port that shadowed the raw input with the generated string could not reproduce for either input.

One name in both scopes: the selector reads the caller's numeric value while the template interpolates the generated word the selector produced. It pins both halves of the scope rule at once — a port that let raw input win at interpolation would render the number, and a port that shadowed it during selection would fail to resolve at all.
The modern spelling as the control for the iw cases: without it a port could pass them by resolving everything to the fallback.
Deprecated in as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale route.
Deprecated in through a constant localeSupplier; supplierCalls reports the rewritten id.
Deprecated in through the supplied-match ingress: identical to the per-call-locale route bar supplierCalls, for the same reason as iw.
Deprecated in through the supplied-match ingress on the range-list solver; requestedLanguageRanges carries in and id.
The same spelling as a parsed header: identical selection and chain, but requestedLanguageRanges carries in and id. The IANA expansion is visible only in that channel.
Deprecated in as a per-call locale against loaded id: rewritten to id by Locale.forLanguageTag, so EXACT/id with range id and chain [id].
Deprecated iw as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale route, which is what makes the instance ingress substitutable for it.

Deprecated iw through a constant localeSupplier. supplierCalls reports he — the tag AFTER Locale.forLanguageTag has had its say — which is where the JDK rewrite layer is separated from the library's own canonicalization.

Deprecated iw negotiated inside a localeSupplier. The result's match is DERIVED from the collapsed Locale, so the ranges reported are the selection's own tag (he) rather than the iw, he expansion the supplier actually used — the observable cost of the collapse, against the match-supplier route on the identical header.

Deprecated iw through the supplied-match ingress. MEASURED identical to the per-call-locale route bar supplierCalls: the JDK rewrite happens before either route, so the request already IS the loaded locale and the supplied match's locale is the same tag. The negative control for the mo/sh rows, where the supplied match does move the lookup.

Deprecated iw through the supplied-match ingress on the range-list solver. requestedLanguageRanges carries iw and he — the equivalence expansion the single-locale kernel never performs — proving the two solvers are fed differently even where they agree on the selection.

The same spelling as a parsed header, which goes through the pinned IANA equivalence table instead of through Locale.forLanguageTag. MEASURED: same EXACT/he selection and same chain, but requestedLanguageRanges carries BOTH iw and he. The ranges channel is the only place the two layers are distinguishable for this spelling.

The SAME spelling as an explicitly constructed range rather than a parsed header. new LanguageRange('iw') adds no IANA equivalents, so this route offers only iw — and MEASURED the match degrades from EXACT/he (header form, which also offers he) to CANONICAL/he with range iw. If a port implements languageRanges by always parsing, this case and its header twin collapse into one and the distinction is lost.

Deprecated iw as a per-call locale against loaded he. Locale.forLanguageTag rewrites iw to he BEFORE the library sees it, so the request arrives already canonical: EXACT/he, range he, chain [he]. Identical to the he control below, which is the assertion.
The same alias question isolated from resolution: matchFor(Locale mo) yields CANONICAL/ro with languageRange mo and a single requested range. Paired with the header form below.

matchFor('mo') yields EXACT/ro with languageRange ro and requested ranges mo, ro. MEASURED: the two solvers DISAGREE on this spelling. ingress-smoke establishes that the kernel and the list solver produce byte-identical blocks for zh-TW; this pair is the counterexample that stops a port from generalizing that to all inputs.

A file named mo, requested as canonical ro through a constant localeSupplier. Compare with the per-call-locale ro case on the same catalog: same question, same answer, and supplierCalls proves which ingress asked.
A file named mo, requested as mo through the supplied-match ingress: EXACT/mo, chain [mo], plus the supplierCalls record.

The same canonical request as a header. LanguageRange.parse('ro') emits ro and its equivalent mo, so the match is EXACT/mo with ranges ro, mo and the lookup locale is mo — not the CANONICAL/mo at lookupLocale ro the per-call-locale route reports. Both routes reach the catalog; they disagree on how they say so.

A request for mo against a FILE named mo: the exact-identity path, EXACT/mo, not the alias path. Pairs with ingress-matrix-java.alias.mo-per-call-locale, where the same request must travel through canonicalization to reach a file named ro.

The canonical spelling against a catalog that exists only under the deprecated one. MEASURED: it DOES reach it — CANONICAL/mo, lookupLocale ro, chain [mo] — so canonicalization runs in both directions even though the loader applies no alias at all.
Deprecated mo as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale route, lookupLocale mo and all.

Deprecated mo through a constant localeSupplier. supplierCalls reports mo UNCHANGED — Locale.forLanguageTag does not rewrite it — which is the direct contrast with the iw row's supplierCalls reporting he.

Deprecated mo negotiated inside a localeSupplier: MEASURED EXACT/ro with the single range ro, where the match supplier on the same header reports EXACT/ro with ranges mo, ro. The selection survives the collapse; the negotiation history does not.
Deprecated mo through the supplied-match ingress: the CANONICAL/ro match is preserved but the lookup locale becomes ro, where the per-call-locale route keeps mo. Same chain, different lookup locale.

Deprecated mo through the supplied-match ingress on the range-list solver: EXACT/ro with ranges mo, ro, against the kernel route's CANONICAL/ro with range mo. The sharpest solver disagreement in the alias arm, carried onto the resolution channel.

The same spelling as a parsed header. MEASURED: the IANA table supplies ro as a second range, so the match is EXACT/ro with range ro (not CANONICAL/ro with range mo) and the lookup locale is ro rather than mo. This is the one spelling where the equivalence table changes the match TYPE, not just the reported ranges.

mo as a constructed range with no equivalence expansion. MEASURED CANONICAL/ro with range mo, against the header form's EXACT/ro with range ro on the identical catalog — so whatever reaches ro here does so through the library's own canonicalization, not through the table.

Deprecated mo as a per-call locale against loaded ro. Locale.forLanguageTag does NOT rewrite mo, so it arrives as the Locale mo and only CLDR canonicalization inside the matcher reaches ro: MEASURED lookupLocale mo, match CANONICAL/ro with range mo, chain [ro]. Compare the ro control, which is EXACT.
The modern spelling as the control for the mo cases: ro is loaded, so this is EXACT, and the CANONICAL the mo cases report is attributable to the alias rather than to the catalog.
Deprecated sh as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale route, including the [sh, sr-Latn, en] chain.
Deprecated sh through a constant localeSupplier: supplierCalls reports sh unchanged, and the derived NONE match still leaves the three-step chain intact.

sh through the supplied-match ingress. The match is NONE, so DefaultStrings.java:2453 takes the lookup locale from the match's FALLBACK locale and the chain becomes just [en] — while the per-call-locale route walks sh and sr-Latn first. The sharpest attempted-chain divergence in the family.

sh through the supplied-match ingress on the range-list solver. sh has no IANA entry, so the expanded list is the single range sh — the negative control for iw/in/mo, where the same route reports two ranges — and the lookup still collapses to the fallback because the match is NONE.

sh as a parsed header. sh has NO entry in the pinned IANA table, so the range list is the same single range as the Locale route's and the diagnostic is the same NONE — but the lookup locale comes from the empty match and collapses to the fallback, so the chain loses sh and sr-Latn. Same ranges, same diagnostic, different chain: the difference here is purely the ingress.

Deprecated sh as a per-call locale against loaded sr. The matcher finds nothing — CLDR's alias target is sr-Latn and only sr is on disk — so the diagnostic channel reports NONE, yet the RESOLUTION channel still walks [sh, sr-Latn, en] and serves en. The two channels disagree completely here, which is what makes the spelling worth an ingress sweep.
Deprecated tl as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale route, lookupLocale tl and all.
Deprecated tl through a constant localeSupplier: supplierCalls reports tl unchanged, and the derived match is CANONICAL/fil.
Deprecated tl through the supplied-match ingress: CANONICAL/fil preserved, lookup locale becomes fil where the per-call-locale route keeps tl.

tl through the supplied-match ingress on the range-list solver. Like sh, tl has no IANA equivalent so the range list stays single; unlike sh it still reaches loaded fil as CANONICAL. The pair separates the JDK equivalence table from the library's own canonicalization in one comparison.

tl as a parsed header. With no IANA equivalent the ranges are identical to the Locale route's and so is the CANONICAL/fil match; the ONLY difference is the lookup locale (fil, not tl). Pairs with the mo header case, where the table does change the match — together they separate the equivalence table from the ingress rule.

Deprecated tl as a per-call locale against loaded fil. Locale.forLanguageTag leaves tl alone and the IANA table has no entry, so only CLDR's tl to fil alias can reach the catalog: MEASURED lookupLocale tl, CANONICAL/fil with range tl, chain [fil].
EN-us as the ambient instance locale; must agree with the per-call-locale spelling case on every channel.
EN-us through a constant localeSupplier: the derived-match route, which keeps en-US as the lookup locale and so keeps the two-step chain.

EN-us through the supplied-match ingress: the lookup locale is the match's en, so the chain is [en] against the localeSupplier route's [en-US, en] on the identical catalog. Same requested spelling, same selection, different chain.
EN-us as a per-call range list: the lookup becomes the selected en, so the chain loses the en-US entry — case normalization and the ingress difference measured in one call.
EN-us as a per-call locale against seed row 5's lone en. Must equal the canonical en-US case exactly, including the CLDR_FALLBACK diagnostic and the two-step chain.
The canonical spelling, control for the whole mixed-case arm. Without it a port could pass every mixed-case case by being uniformly wrong.
ZH-hant as the ambient instance locale, no per-call argument; must agree with the per-call-locale spelling case.
ZH-hant through a constant localeSupplier. supplierCalls records the tag the supplier actually handed over, already normalized to zh-Hant — where a port that normalizes late becomes visible.

ZH-hant negotiated inside a localeSupplier and collapsed to a bare Locale. Because the selection is an EXACT match on the requested tag, the collapse loses nothing here — the negative control for the seed rows, where it loses the diagnostic.

ZH-hant through the supplied-match ingress. MEASURED: identical to the per-call-locale route on every channel except supplierCalls, because zh-Hant is loaded and the match is EXACT, so the lookup locale the supplied match hands over is the tag the per-call route would have used anyway. This is the control showing the supplied-match lookup difference in the seed rows comes from the match SELECTING a different locale, not from the ingress itself.

ZH-hant through the supplied-match ingress via the whole-list solver. The pinned IANA table has no entry for zh-hant, so the expanded list is a single range and this must be identical to the single-locale-kernel case — the negative control for the alias and extlang arms, where expansion does change the reported ranges.

ZH-hant as a per-call range list. The case pins that agreement; a port lowercasing only on the header path, or echoing ZH-hant into either channel, breaks here.

What it records is the Java BUILDER's ordering, and coverage-dispositions.json already classifies that cross-clearing side-effect as nonportable (TranslationOptions$Builder :310/:312/:330/:332, 'a nullable setter on a MUTABLE BUILDER, which the port does not have'). A JS per-call options object literal has no application order -- spread order would be the same accident -- so plan 8.2's rule that every requiredPortableId passes with an EMPTY unsupported set could not be satisfied by any port once both orders are in the corpus. The port-side obligation is unchanged and lives where it belongs: the permanent `required` disposition on TranslationOptions#<init>:70.

cases.notes: In lenient mode an unbound placeholder is re-emitted with its delimiters and recorded in unresolvedPlaceholderNames instead of raising, while a neighbouring escape is still processed in the same pass (so the output differs from the key by the collapsed backslash and the catch-all cannot mask it). If absent, a JS port could drop or blank unbound placeholders, destroying the diagnostic value of the returned key, and the strict counterpart - where the same condition becomes a RESOLUTION_FAILURE - would be the only behavior pinned.

Pins the FIRST branch of StringInterpolator's escape handling (StringInterpolator.java:108-112): a backslash followed by a backslash consumes both (index += 2) and emits exactly one. If absent, a JS port that treats the backslash as a pure lookahead marker (peek, then keep the marker, index += 1) emits two backslashes, and every Windows path, regex, or LaTeX fragment in a catalog doubles on every render.

Replacement values are appended to the output buffer and never rescanned, so caller-supplied data containing escape syntax survives byte for byte (verified: the doubled backslash stays doubled and the escaped opening stays escaped). If absent, a JS port that runs a single escape pass over the finished string would corrupt any user data containing backslashes or braces - a data-integrity and injection concern, not a cosmetic one. The value is a bare JSON string, which per plan section 3.7 is always text and never reinterpreted.

Two backslashes escape each other and leave the following placeholder REAL, so 'name' is required and substituted (one backslash then Ada). This is the exact counterpart of the single-backslash escape and the pair is what distinguishes 'escape the escape' from 'escape the placeholder'. If absent, a JS port could treat any backslash run before '{{' as suppressing the placeholder.

ADDED IN REVIEW. The three-character advance of the escaped-close branch landing exactly on string.length(). The sibling case has trailing text, so an off-by-one that re-reads or drops the final brace pair would still pass it; this one is the only case where the loop must terminate immediately after that branch.

Backslash before a closing delimiter emits the two closing braces and consumes THREE characters (index += 1 + PLACEHOLDER_END.length()). If absent, a JS port would either keep the backslash in the output or, because an unescaped '}}' throws in strict mode, reject a perfectly legal translation at render time.

ADDED IN REVIEW. The CLOSED escaped-open branch advancing to exactly string.length() (index = escapedPlaceholderEnd + 2 == length). The clause names 'closed and unclosed' escaped openings; the unclosed one already has its own end-of-string case, but the closed one's terminating advance was untested. A binding for 'name' is supplied so a port that substitutes rather than copies is caught here too.

Inside an escaped region the text between the delimiters is never checked against LocalizedStringUtils.isValidLocalizedStringIdentifier, so '1:2' passes both LocalizedStringLoader's load-time strict scan and strict interpolation. If absent, a JS port that validated escaped text would reject a catalog Java loads, turning a rendering nicety into a startup failure.

The same translation with NO bindings at all. Because placeholderNamesIn skips escaped regions, 'name' is never added to unresolvedPlaceholderNames and interpolateTemplate must NOT raise the 'Missing value for placeholder(s)' error (DefaultStrings.java:1379) it raises for real ones. Verified to emit status TRANSLATED, not RETURNED_KEY. If absent, a JS port that collects names with a naive regex would fail a translation Java renders fine, and the failure would surface as a resolution failure rather than a visible bug.

When no closing delimiter exists anywhere after an escaped opening, the interpolator appends everything from just after the backslash to end of string and breaks. Crucially this does NOT throw, unlike an unescaped unclosed placeholder in strict mode. If absent, a JS port would likely raise 'Unclosed placeholder' on a translation Java renders happily - and, because that translation also has to survive the loader's strict scan, would fail at startup rather than at render.

The whole point of the escape: a value IS bound for 'name', and the escaped placeholder must still render literally rather than interpolate. If absent, a JS port that strips backslashes before scanning for placeholders would substitute Ada and destroy any documentation string that shows placeholder syntax to the reader.

The escaped-opening branch scans forward for the NEXT '}}' anywhere in the string, not for a matching one, so an escaped opening with no close of its own consumes a later REAL placeholder into the literal region - the bound value for realName is ignored and the braces are emitted verbatim. Confirmed by the oracle. This is the highest-risk trap in the escape grammar; if absent, a JS port that scoped the escape to the adjacent token would interpolate Ada and diverge on a legal, loadable catalog.

A generated language-form fragment is itself interpolated (its escape becomes literal braces) and the RESULT is then spliced into the outer template as a replacement value, not rescanned - so the literal braces survive even though the outer template does bind 'name' (verified output combines a literal {{name}} from the fragment with a substituted Ada from the outer template). If absent, a JS port that re-interpolates expanded fragments would substitute Ada into text Java leaves literal. REVIEW FIX: count is now a tagged integer so the CARDINALITY_ONE selection cannot hinge on the driver's number decoding.

ADDED IN REVIEW - a branch the original set left entirely uncovered. The escaped-open branch copies string[start,end) in ONE appendChecked call with no recursion, so escape sequences INSIDE the region are not processed: the doubled backslash inside 'Region \{{a \\ b}} kept' stays doubled in the output. Verified against the oracle. If absent, a JS port that re-ran its escape scanner over the literal region would collapse it, and nothing else in the family would notice. Corollary proved by probe: an escaped '\}}' inside such a region does NOT protect it (the region ends at that very '}}'), leaving a bare '}}' that makes the translation unloadable - see the lenient twin of this case, where the same string is observable.

ADDED IN REVIEW. A declared language-form placeholder whose ONLY reference in the template sits inside an escaped region. Verified: the catalog loads (the loader does not require a declared placeholder to be referenced), 'label' never appears in placeholderNamesIn, the generated fragment is never selected or expanded, and the output is the literal braces. This pins that placeholderNamesIn - the same function used by the loader's reference check, by enqueueGeneratedPlaceholderDependencies, and by interpolateTemplate's context assembly - agrees about escaped regions in all three roles. If absent, a JS port could expand the form anyway (rendering 'one book') or reject the catalog as declaring an unused placeholder.

A backslash preceding anything other than a backslash, '{{', or '}}' is emitted verbatim and only ONE character is consumed (the final fall-through branch, StringInterpolator.java:134-136). The translation uses backslash-t twice, so a port built on a JSON- or C-style unescaper would swallow the backslash or turn it into a tab, silently corrupting path-like translations.

The bound twin of the previous case over the IDENTICAL translation, isolating the binding as the only difference (TRANSLATED, with the escaped close still collapsed to literal braces). Without it the failure case could be misread as escape mishandling rather than a missing value, and a JS port could 'fix' the wrong thing.
