parse.failureMessage: object-empty: either a translation or at least one alternative expression is required for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: An empty object value: no unknown members, but nothing to translate either. Pins the 'translation or at least one alternative' requirement, which a port special-casing {} as an empty translation would violate.

parse.failureMessage: object-translation-number: translation must be a string for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: 'translation' present but a number. Distinct from the value-type family: here the entry IS an object, so the error names the translation member rather than the entry.

parse.failureMessage: object-translation-null: translation must be a string for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: 'translation': null. Verified to produce the wrong-TYPE message, not the absent-member message: the loader's guard is `!= null` on the JSON member, then isString(). A port using `if (obj.translation)` would take the absent branch and report 'either a translation or at least one alternative expression is required' instead.

parse.failureMessage: object-unknown-member: unexpected field 'note' in localized string for key 'Key.A'. Valid fields are [alternatives, commentary, placeholders, translation]

cases.notes: An unknown member alongside a valid translation. Pins that the loader is strict rather than tolerant, and pins the enumerated, sorted set of valid localized-string fields carried in the message: [alternatives, commentary, placeholders, translation].

parse.failureMessage: placeholders-array: the placeholders value must be an object. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: 'placeholders' as an array. A JS port using typeof === 'object' accepts arrays and would then iterate zero named placeholders; Java rejects the file. The check runs before the translation's own {{books}} reference is resolved, so this file isolates one cause.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-definition-string: the placeholder value must be an object. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A placeholder definition that is a bare string. Pins that there is no string shorthand for a placeholder definition, and that the message names the KEY rather than the placeholder.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-definition-empty: placeholder 'books' for root key 'Key.A' must define either a language-form translation or a template translation

cases.notes: An empty placeholder definition declares neither placeholder mode. Pins the error that names both member sets, which is the only message stating the two-mode model.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-name-invalid: invalid placeholder '1books'. Placeholder names must start with a Unicode letter or underscore and contain only Unicode letters, Unicode numbers, Unicode combining marks, underscores, or hyphens. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A placeholder named '1books', which the identifier grammar forbids. The translation deliberately does NOT reference it, so the case pins that the name is checked on the DEFINITION even when nothing uses it.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-modes-mixed: placeholder 'books' for root key 'Key.A' mixes language-form members [value, range, translations] with template members [translation, alternatives]; placeholder modes are mutually exclusive

cases.notes: A definition carrying both language-form members (value/translations) and a template member (translation). Pins that the two placeholder modes are mutually exclusive rather than merged or precedence-ordered, and that this check precedes every per-mode check.

parse.failureMessage: placeholders-null: the placeholders value must be an object. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: 'placeholders': null. The sharpest JS trap in the family, because typeof null === 'object': a port that accepts it then calls Object.entries(null) and either throws an unrelated TypeError or silently sees no placeholders. Verified to emit the same must-be-an-object message as the array form.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-name-reserved: invalid placeholder 'CARDINALITY_ONE'. Placeholder names may not use reserved expression constants. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A placeholder named CARDINALITY_ONE. A valid identifier, but reserved as an expression constant -- a port checking only the identifier regex would accept it and then shadow a language-form constant inside expressions. Pins the second, distinct branch of the same name check.

parse.failureMessage: placeholder-definition-unknown-member: unexpected field 'extra' in placeholder 'books' for key 'Key.A'. Valid fields are [alternatives, range, translation, translations, value]

cases.notes: An unknown member inside an otherwise valid placeholder definition. Pins the enumerated valid placeholder members [alternatives, range, translation, translations, value], which differ from the localized-string members -- two whitelists a port could easily merge into one.

Control for this whole fixture: a well-formed placeholder the translation never references LOADS, with no warning (sv is one/other so the cardinality table is complete). Without it a port could pass every rejection above by rejecting any unreferenced definition, and it isolates the name rule in the two preceding cases from an unused-placeholder rule that does not exist.

parse.failureMessage: range-end-number: a placeholder translation range end must be a string. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A numeric range END, behind a valid string start so the end branch is actually reached. Pins the symmetric check: a port that validated only the start would accept this file.

parse.failureMessage: range-missing-end: a placeholder translation range end is required. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A range with only a start. Pins that both endpoints are mandatory rather than the missing one defaulting to open-ended.

parse.failureMessage: range-string: the placeholder translation range must be an object. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: 'range' as a string. Pins that there is no 'lo..hi' shorthand for a range.

parse.failureMessage: range-start-null: a placeholder translation range start is required. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: An explicitly null range start. Verified to be FOLDED INTO the same 'range start is required' message as an absent start -- the guard is `start == null || start.isNull()`. Paired with malformed-structure.range.end-required, which reaches that same wording by absence, this pins that null and missing are ONE case inside the range object, unlike the placeholder members one level up where they are two. A JS port testing `'start' in range` would accept explicit null.

parse.failureMessage: range-start-number: a placeholder translation range start must be a string. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A numeric range start. Endpoints name INPUT placeholders, not values, so a number is a type error rather than a literal bound -- a port treating ranges as numeric intervals would accept it.

parse.failureMessage: range-start-bad-identifier: invalid range start '1lo'. Placeholder names must start with a Unicode letter or underscore and contain only Unicode letters, Unicode numbers, Unicode combining marks, underscores, or hyphens. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A range start of '1lo': correctly typed, but not a legal identifier. Pins a third, distinct message on the same member and pins that range endpoints go through the placeholder identifier grammar -- direct evidence for the claim that endpoints name inputs rather than values.

parse.failureMessage: range-unknown-member: unexpected field 'step' in range for placeholder 'books' for key 'Key.A'. Valid fields are [end, start]

cases.notes: An unknown 'step' member. Pins the range object's own member whitelist [end, start], which is narrower than the placeholder's -- a third whitelist a port must keep separate.
Control: the same shape with both endpoints as strings loads and reports its key. Proves the preceding rejections are about the specific violation and not about ranges generally.

parse.failureMessage: reference-in-alternative: invalid placeholder reference in translation declared at Key.A -> alternative[count == 0] for key 'Key.A': Malformed placeholder '{{1bad}}'. Placeholder names must start with a Unicode letter or underscore and contain only Unicode letters, Unicode numbers, Unicode combining marks, underscores, or hyphens

cases.notes: A malformed reference inside an alternative. Pins the 'declared at <rootKey> -> alternative[<expression>]' path rendering, which no other case in the corpus reaches and which a port must reproduce to make deep catalogs debuggable. Also pins that the reported key stays the ROOT key while the path carries the location.

parse.failureMessage: reference-in-placeholder-translation: invalid placeholder reference in placeholder translation for generated placeholder 'books' for key 'Key.A': Malformed placeholder '{{1bad}}'. Placeholder names must start with a Unicode letter or underscore and contain only Unicode letters, Unicode numbers, Unicode combining marks, underscores, or hyphens

cases.notes: A malformed reference inside a language-form translation value. Pins that nested templates are checked too, and pins the description text naming the generated placeholder that owns the template.

parse.failureMessage: reference-malformed-name: invalid placeholder reference in translation for key 'Key.A': Malformed placeholder '{{1bad}}'. Placeholder names must start with a Unicode letter or underscore and contain only Unicode letters, Unicode numbers, Unicode combining marks, underscores, or hyphens

cases.notes: '{{1bad}}' in a translation. The SAME construction is left as a literal at interpolation time -- interpolation-escapes.lenient.malformed-placeholder-name-is-literal renders '{{2bad}}' verbatim -- so this pins that load-time reference checking is STRICT while lenient interpolation is not. A port sharing one interpolator for both phases will get exactly one of the two wrong.

parse.failureMessage: reference-reserved-constant: invalid translation placeholder reference 'CARDINALITY_ONE'. Placeholder names may not use reserved expression constants. Key is 'Key.A'

cases.notes: '{{CARDINALITY_ONE}}' as a reference. A well-formed identifier that is nonetheless reserved; pins the reserved-name check on the REFERENCE path, not just on definitions, and its distinct message wording ('invalid translation placeholder reference').

parse.failureMessage: reference-stray-close: invalid placeholder reference in translation for key 'Key.A': Unexpected placeholder closing delimiter '}}' at index 6

cases.notes: A '}}' with no opening. Pins a distinct strict-mode error from the unclosed case, catching a port that only scans for opening delimiters.

parse.failureMessage: reference-unclosed: invalid placeholder reference in translation for key 'Key.A': Unclosed placeholder starting at index 7

cases.notes: '{{name' with no closing delimiter. Pins strict load-time rejection of an unclosed placeholder, including the reported character index -- while its lenient counterpart emits the remainder instead of failing.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-array: a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object

cases.notes: A top-level JSON array. Pins the single-JSON-object requirement, which a port doing Object.entries(parsed) would miss because arrays enumerate too.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-empty: a localized strings file may not be blank; use an empty JSON object ({}) for an empty file

cases.notes: A zero-byte file. Pins that empty is treated as blank rather than as an empty catalog -- a port defaulting to {} would load it silently and lose the operator's mistake.

The control for the blank cases: an explicit empty object is a VALID catalog with zero keys, exactly as the blank-file message advises. Without this a port could pass by rejecting everything blank-ish.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-nbsp:1:1: unable to parse localized strings file

cases.notes: A file containing only U+00A0. Verified to take the PARSE-ERROR path with a line:column, not the blank path: the loader's blank test accepts exactly space, tab, LF and CR (isJsonWhitespaceOnly), unlike Java's String.isBlank() or JS's String.prototype.trim(), both of which would call this file blank and emit the wrong message. This is the case that pins the boundary the previous one only samples from inside.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-null: a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object

cases.notes: A top-level JSON null. The typeof-null trap at document scope: JSON.parse('null') returns null and typeof null === 'object', so a naive JS port's object check passes and the file is accepted as an empty catalog. Java reports the same not-an-object error as an array.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-number: a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object

cases.notes: A top-level JSON number. Distinguishes the not-an-object error from the syntax error a stricter parser might raise instead.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-string: a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object

cases.notes: A top-level JSON string. Pins the same requirement for a scalar document.

parse.failureMessage: top-level-whitespace: a localized strings file may not be blank; use an empty JSON object ({}) for an empty file

cases.notes: A file containing all four characters the loader treats as JSON whitespace -- space, tab, LF and CR -- and nothing else. Pins a DEDICATED blank-file message emitted BEFORE JSON parsing, not the parser's own syntax error.

Control: with the variable bound the alternative matches and wins over the parent translation. Proves the alternative is reachable, so the preceding case measures evaluation of an unbound variable and not a broken catalog.

Control for the preceding case: the entry is not defective, only unbound. Distinguishes a deferred failure from a latent structural error, which a port could otherwise satisfy by always failing this key.

The load half of the deferred-failure clause: an undeclared placeholder reference and an alternative expression over an unbound variable are NOT load-time errors, and emit no warning. A port that resolved references or bound expression variables eagerly would fail startup here, turning a per-request failure into an outage.

failures.causeMessage: No value was provided for placeholder 'bookCount'
failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Books' for locale 'en'. Reason: RESOLUTION_FAILURE. Attempted locales: [en]

failureCause.message: No value was provided for placeholder 'bookCount'

cases.notes: An alternative expression over an unbound variable, evaluated at lookup. Pins whether it throws, counts as a non-match, or falls through to the parent translation -- three plausible port behaviors with identical load-time output. Verified to carry a DIFFERENT cause type (com.lokalized.ExpressionEvaluationException) than the unbound-placeholder case, which a port is likely to collapse into one error.

failures.causeMessage: Missing value for placeholder(s) [name] in key 'Greeting'
failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Greeting' for locale 'en'. Reason: RESOLUTION_FAILURE. Attempted locales: [en]

failureCause.message: Missing value for placeholder(s) [name] in key 'Greeting'

cases.notes: The lookup half: the same entry that loaded cleanly now fails per-request as RESOLUTION_FAILURE. Pins the failure reason, the cause TYPE (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException) and its message, and the text the result still carries.

parse.failureMessage: value-type-array: either a translation string or object value is required for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A translation value that is a JSON array. A JS port branching on typeof value === 'object' would mistake an array for the object form and report a different error, or none. Verified to reach the same terminal else-branch message as the other three types, which is itself the portable fact.

parse.failureMessage: value-type-boolean: either a translation string or object value is required for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A translation value that is a JSON boolean. A port using truthiness or String(value) would accept it and produce the text 'true'.

parse.failureMessage: value-type-null: either a translation string or object value is required for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A translation value that is explicit JSON null. typeof null === 'object' in JS, so a port must not let null fall into the object branch; Java routes it to the same terminal else-branch as a number.

parse.failureMessage: value-type-number: either a translation string or object value is required for key 'Key.A'

cases.notes: A translation value that is a JSON number. Pins that the loader rejects it at parse rather than coercing it to '42'.

Requesting the very tag whose file is on disk but undiscovered. Verified attempted de-AT, de, en with no German catalog anywhere in the chain, and the fallback translation returned. A port that indexed catalogs by filename rather than by discovered locale would serve the German file here.

The proof that the German tiebreaker entry is OMITTED rather than present. Verified attemptedLocales is exactly de then en, and matchFor reports NONE. A port that seeded tiebreakerLocalesByLanguageCode from the requested manifest instead of from what actually loaded would hold de:[de,de-AT], and localeFallbackCandidates would then splice a German locale into the attempted list. The paired one-child fixture shows exactly that longer list when de-CH really does load.

Verified: with both de and de-AT loaded and an explicit tiebreaker permutation, an exact request stops at de-AT — attemptedLocales is the single element de-AT and no parent is consulted. A port that always walks the parent chain would report de-AT then de.

fr loaded successfully but does not carry this key. Verified attempted fr then en, resolved en, while the matcher still selects fr EXACTLY. A port that decides fallback per-locale rather than per-key would stop at fr and fail.

Verified: de-CH is not in the manifest and reaches the loaded de catalog by CLDR fallback (attempted de-CH then de), NOT diverted to the sibling de-AT by the tiebreaker list. Discriminates a port that treats the tiebreaker list as a preference order applied before parent fallback.

Added by review, and the sharpest two-channel case in the family: verified that the matcher selects fr with matchType EXACT (fr genuinely loaded) while resolution walks fr then en and resolves in en. Selection and resolution disagree about a locale that IS in the manifest. A port that derives the diagnostic channel from where the translation came from collapses these two answers into one.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'No.Such.Key' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: Key absent from the only catalog there is. Verified terminal shape: status RETURNED_KEY, translation equal to the key, resolvedLocale null, attemptedLocales [en], while the matcher still selects en EXACTLY. Distinguishes 'no catalog matched' from 'catalog matched, key missing'.

With a single-locale manifest, verified a request for an unrelated locale still records fr in attemptedLocales before resolving in en, while the matcher selects nothing (NONE). A port that short-circuits to the fallback when only one locale is loaded would emit a one-element attempted list.

The directory contains a dot-prefixed en-GB file. Verified the request walks en-GB, en-001, en and returns the en translation, proving the hidden file contributed nothing. A port that skips hidden files only by an extension check, or not at all, returns the hidden file's text instead.

Because exactly one German locale loaded, DefaultStrings synthesizes the identity tiebreaker de:[de-CH]; verified a bare de request reaches de-CH, returns Gruezi, and reports attempted de then de-CH with the matcher selecting de-CH by LIKELY_SUBTAG. Directly opposite to the absent-language fixture, where the same request never leaves de then en. The pair is what makes 'omitted' observable.

de-AT is neither loaded nor the likely-subtag expansion of the loaded de-CH, so the only route to a German catalog is the synthesized tiebreaker plus the likely-language-script check. Verified attempted de-AT, de, de-CH. A port that populates the tiebreaker map but skips the script compatibility test, or vice versa, changes this list.
The key fr is missing. Verified attempted fr then en, resolved en, translated from the fallback catalog. Together with the sibling case this proves partiality is per key, not per locale.

Control for the previous case on the same fixture: the key fr does have is served by fr with attemptedLocales of length one and isFallback false. A port that consults the fallback unconditionally would show fr then en here too.

Added by review, and the case that gives the omitted-entry pair its force: the entry's CONTENT is observable, not just its presence. de-AT is written first and sorts first; the tiebreaker list names de-CH first. Verified the request resolves to de-CH with attempted de-DE, de, de-CH. Seed row 2 (direct-fr-be) cannot catch this — there the tiebreaker order and the file order agree, so a port following manifest insertion order passes it and fails here.

Because de-XX loaded, German DOES get an identity tiebreaker entry, so a bare de request reaches de-XX (attempted de, de-XX) rather than the fallback. The mirror image of the absent-language case: entries follow the loaded set even when the loaded tag is unusual.
The accepted odd tag is a first-class loaded locale: verified an exact request resolves there with a one-element attempted list and matchType EXACT, not through the fallback.

The canonicalized locale is usable end to end: verified a lowercase request resolves against the uppercase-named file with a one-element attempted list. A port that compares filenames case-sensitively would find no catalog and fail to build at all.

The complete-manifest control. Four extensionless files, four locales, and per-locale key lists that differ (en alone carries Only.En). A port that discovers files but drops the per-locale key partition, or that merges catalogs across locales at load time, produces a different keysByLocale here.

The extreme partial load: a non-empty directory whose every entry is skipped yields an EMPTY manifest, successfully, with no warnings. Pins that an empty result is not itself an error at the loader layer. The fixture is loadOnly because Strings construction is what refuses a zero-locale catalog.
The minimal loadable manifest: one file, which is also the fallback. Pins the degenerate end of the manifest range that the multi-locale cases anchor the other end of.

Added by review. fr's file is a valid but empty JSON object. Verified: the manifest still lists fr, with an EMPTY key array — the loader does not drop a zero-key catalog, and does not warn. A port that filters empty catalogs out of the manifest, or that treats an empty object as a parse failure, diverges on the very first field.

Added by review, and the only case in the corpus touching maximumLocalizedStringsFiles — a limit that is squarely about manifest size. Verified: with the cap at 1 and one loadable file among five entries, the load SUCCEEDS. The cap is charged in beginLocalizedStringsFile, which only runs for files that are actually parsed; skipped entries are charged instead to maximumDiscoveryEntries. A port that decrements one budget per directory entry fails here while passing every other case in this family.

load.failureMessage: <fixtures>/manifest-loads-file-limit-exceeded/en: localized strings load exceeds the aggregate localized strings file limit of 1

cases.notes: Added by review as the enforcement half of the previous case: the same cap of 1 against two loadable files aborts the entire directory load, so the skipped-entries case cannot be passed by a port that simply never enforces the limit. Informational for the same reason as the duplicate-spelling case — verified stable across runs here, but the message names whichever of the two files the directory stream reached second, which no implementation controls.

Four extensionless names that are not loadable locale tags: a dotted name that fails the tag grammar, a well-formed but unassigned two-letter code, an ordinary English word that is grammatically a language subtag, and a dot-prefixed file. Verified all are skipped SILENTLY with no warning and no failure, leaving en alone. A port that accepts any well-formed subtag without checking it against the CLDR language set would load two extra locales here.

load.failureMessage: File 'strings.json' ends with .json but is not named with a valid IETF BCP 47 language tag. Use names like 'en', 'en.json', or 'en-US.json'

cases.notes: The same stem that is silently skipped without an extension becomes a hard load failure when it ends in .json, with a message naming the file and suggesting valid names. Verified the diagnostic quotes the bare filename only, so it does not depend on where the fixture was materialized. This asymmetry is the single most likely thing a port gets wrong: skip-vs-reject turns on the extension, not on the name.

The section 8.3 sharp clause. Both German files sit in the directory but neither is discovered, so the load succeeds with en and fr only, emits ZERO warnings, and German appears nowhere in locales or keysByLocale. A port that reports a partially-loaded German, or that warns about undiscovered files, diverges here.

The contrast fixture: the de file is unrecognized but de-CH loads, so German contributes exactly one locale. Pins that a language is represented by whatever survived discovery, not by the set of files placed for it.

load.failureMessage: <fixtures>/manifest-loads-non-object-root/de: a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object

cases.notes: Added by review. A second, distinct way for one file to kill the directory load: valid JSON whose root is an array. Verified the diagnostic is 'a localized strings file must be comprised of a single JSON object' with no line:column, which separates root-shape rejection from syntax rejection. Without this pair a port could implement one message for both and match neither precisely.

A deliberately partial manifest: fr is present but carries one of the three keys en carries. The load observation shows the asymmetric key lists rather than a union. A port that pre-merges catalogs into the fallback at load time cannot reproduce this.
Added by review. The load control for the order case: both German children really are in the manifest, so the following case cannot be explained by one of them being absent.

A directory holding one file, for a locale that is not the configured fallback. Verified loading succeeds and reports fr; the loader does not know or care about the fallback locale. The fixture is loadOnly because Strings construction is what rejects the missing fallback, and that rejection belongs to a different channel.

load.failureMessage: Duplicate localized strings file for locale 'en' found at '<fixtures>/manifest-loads-duplicate-locale-spellings/en'

cases.notes: An extensionless en and an en.json in one directory resolve to the same Locale and the load fails with a duplicate-file diagnostic. A port keyed by filename would silently accept both and let one win. DEMOTED BY REVIEW from requiredPortableIds: failed, failureType, locales and keysByLocale are all deterministic, but failureMessage quotes whichever entry the directory stream reached SECOND, and that is a filesystem property, not a library property. Measured stable across five runs on APFS — and stable at the file written FIRST, i.e. readdir order is not creation order — so it cannot be pinned as a portable message. Gating parity on it would fail a correct port on any host whose readdir hashes differently.

A surprise worth pinning, and confirmed against the library: de-XX names an unassigned region, yet the loader accepts it and the manifest gains a de-XX locale. Discovery validates the LANGUAGE against CLDR, not the region. A port that validates the whole tag against a known-locale table would skip this file and silently shrink the manifest.

load.failureMessage: <fixtures>/manifest-loads-language-files-unparseable/de:1:27: unable to parse localized strings file

Verified the observation comes back with an empty locale list and a line:column diagnostic naming the German file. A port that skips bad files and returns a partial manifest would pass every other case in this family and still be wrong here.

A file named with an uppercase tag is discovered and reported under the canonical lowercase locale. Pins that the manifest key is the parsed Locale, not the literal filename, which is the mechanism behind the duplicate-spelling collision.

The second channel. With no German locale loaded the matcher selects nothing at all, not the fallback: locale null, matchType NONE, consideredLocales holding only en and fr. Contrast the one-child fixture, where the same request selects a concrete German locale.

Matcher channel counterpart: verified the selection is de-CH with matchType LIKELY_SUBTAG and isMatch true, where the absent-language fixture selects nothing with NONE. Pins that the diagnostic channel is driven by the loaded set too.

Both colliding files are individually parseable — verified — so the load failure is purely about locale identity across filenames, not about content. This half of the proposition is order-independent and stays portable.
Parses the hidden file directly to show the skip is a leading-dot naming rule and not a content rejection — verified to parse cleanly. Isolates the discovery rule from the parse rule.

Feeds the skipped file straight to the parser to prove its contents are a perfectly good catalog — verified to parse to the single key Greeting. The load excluded it purely on its NAME. Without this a port could pass the load case by rejecting the file's content for the wrong reason.

French `many` requires e = 0 and i != 0 and i % 1000000 = 0 and v = 0. 10^17 satisfies it (MANY). Exercises an exact modulus against a million at a magnitude beyond binary64's integer precision, in a rule shape unlike Russian's last-digit tests.
The 10^18 magnitude through the French million-modulus rule (MANY). Kept alongside the 10^17 row because the clause names all three magnitudes explicitly; on its own it is a near-duplicate of 10^17.
The 10^20 magnitude through the French million-modulus rule, beyond 64-bit integer range (MANY). Control for the 10^20 + 1 case.

10^20 + 1 is not divisible by a million, so the oracle records OTHER, but 1e20 + 1 === 1e20 in JavaScript and a `number`-backed port would report many. Pins the French rule's exact remainder arithmetic above the safe-integer boundary.

Russian cardinals read i % 10 and i % 100 with v = 0. MAX_SAFE_INTEGER ends in 91, so it takes ONE at a magnitude where a naive implementation would assume plurality. Pins that i is derived from the exact integer, not from a rounded double.
10^17 with i % 10 = 0, recorded MANY. Anchors the first of the three magnitudes named by the clause in a locale whose rules actually read the last digit of i.
The control for the 10^18 + 1 cases: MANY. Without the pair, the +1 case proves nothing about precision loss.

The mirror of the long 10^18 + 1 case: the same digits as a binary64 collapse to exactly 10^18, so i % 10 becomes 0 and the oracle records MANY. The long/double pair pins the collapse in BOTH directions -- a port that kept full precision for a JS number would report one here, and a port that lost it would report many for the long row. Added in review; the family previously pinned the collapse only in English ordinals.

10^18 + 1 is not representable as a binary64: 1e18 + 1 === 1e18 in JavaScript. Its last digit 1 puts it in ONE while 10^18 itself is MANY, so a port that loses the trailing unit changes the visible category. This is the 10^18 magnitude the clause names, made observable.
10^20 exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE and must travel as an arbitrary-precision integer. Recorded MANY; control for the 10^20 + 1 case.

10^20 + 1 is indistinguishable from 10^20 in binary64 and does not fit a 64-bit integer either, yet the oracle records ONE against MANY for 10^20. The strongest single argument in this family for a bigint-backed operand pipeline: the category flips on a unit a `number` cannot hold.
The immediate successor of MAX_SAFE_INTEGER takes a different Russian category (FEW, via i % 10 = 2). Adjacent integers straddling the safe-integer boundary must not collapse to one answer.

English `one` requires i = 1 and v = 0. The unshifted mantissa satisfies both, the shifted value does not, and the oracle records OTHER. Paired with the Hindi case this proves the shift happens before the operands are derived, in a locale whose rule is sensitive to i rather than to n.

The mirror image: mantissa 0.001 shifted right by 3 becomes exactly 1 with v = 0, so English reports ONE. Unshifted it would be i = 0, v = 3 and `other`. Together with the previous case, the two directions pin the shift; either alone could be satisfied by ignoring the exponent in one direction.

The same mantissa shifted right by one gives n = 10, whose last digit is 0, so the recorded English ordinal category is OTHER. Pins that the compact shift is applied on the ORDINAL operand path too -- a port that honored the exponent only for cardinals would return one here and pass every other compact case in the family.

The control for the ordinal compact-exponent pair: explicit operands with no exponent give n = 1 and English ordinal ONE. Added in review -- nothing else in the corpus reaches Ordinality.forOperands with caller-supplied operands, so the ordinal operand entry point was previously untested.

thrown.message: Compact exponent 65 exceeds the maximum of 64

cases.notes: One past the default maximum. The oracle records IllegalArgumentException("Compact exponent 65 exceeds the maximum of 64"), so a JS port cannot silently accept an unbounded exponent and materialize an arbitrarily large decimal.

French `many` is `e = 0 and i != 0 and i % 1000000 = 0 and v = 0 or e != 0..5`. Exponent 5 is the last value inside the range and the shifted i is 100000, so neither disjunct fires and the oracle records OTHER. Pins the inclusive upper bound of a range condition read directly off the compact exponent.

Exponent 6 is the first value outside 0..5, so MANY fires purely because of e -- with the same mantissa as the exponent-5 case. Pins that c and e equal the compact exponent and are themselves rule inputs, not just bookkeeping.

The other disjunct of the French `many` rule: e = 0, i != 0, i % 1000000 = 0, v = 0. Reaching MANY by a different route than the exponent cases proves the port implements both disjuncts rather than short-circuiting on e.

thrown.message: Compact exponent must be non-negative, but was -1

cases.notes: Compact exponents are non-negative. The oracle records IllegalArgumentException("Compact exponent must be non-negative, but was -1"), pinning rejection rather than a silent left shift that would quietly turn a compact display into a fraction.

64 is TranslationRuntimeLimits.DEFAULT_MAXIMUM_COMPACT_EXPONENT (verified in source), so this is the largest exponent accepted without overriding limits -- no runtime-limit override is used. The oracle records MANY, pinning that the boundary is inclusive and that a 65-digit materialized value classifies normally.
Shifting 1.25 right by two consumes the fraction exactly: n = 125, v = 0, i % 10 = 5, so the oracle records MANY. The partner of the exponent-1 case; one shift step changes the answer.

Shifting 1.25 right by one leaves 12.5 with v = 1. Every Russian cardinal rule demands v = 0, so the leftover visible decimal is directly observable as OTHER. A port that discarded the fraction during the shift would produce i = 12 and report `few`. Pins that the shift subtracts from the scale rather than truncating.
A compact exponent that pushes the value past binary64 integer precision, read by a rule that inspects i % 10 (MANY). Ties the compact-exponent path to the 10^20 magnitude the clause names.

The 10^17 magnitude the clause names, in the third Indic locale, through the translation path ("bn-other"). Added in review: without it the fixture's bn catalog is never selected by any case, so the fixture claimed hi/bn/gu coverage it did not have, and 10^17 was absent from the Indic translation path.

Trailing zeros through the translation path: an exact decimal with one visible place is not English `one`, so "en-other" is returned. Pins that the tagged-decimal wire shape survives DefaultStrings rather than being coerced on the way in.

The same text as a double normalizes to v = 0 and selects "en-one". The pair makes the trailing-zero type contract observable in the returned translation, which is the only channel a consumer of the library actually sees.

A 21-digit literal compared against an arbitrary-precision placeholder, matching "order-ten-to-the-20-plus-one". Pins that numeric literals in alternatives are parsed as exact decimals with no 64-bit or binary64 intermediate, at the 10^20 magnitude the clause names.

An alternative expression comparing against the literal 9007199254740993. Expression literals become exact BigDecimals, so an exact integral placeholder matches and the oracle records "order-two-to-the-53-plus-one". Pins the safe-integer boundary through the alternative-selection path, not only through the classifier.
The control for the 10^20 + 1 alternative: one unit lower and no alternative matches, returning "order-default". Without it the matching case does not prove exactness.

The same digits as a double collapse to 2^53 and do NOT match the ...993 literal, so the base translation "order-default" is returned. This pair is the reason the JS port cannot use `number` for expression operands: a single numeric type makes these two calls indistinguishable, yet they must return different translations.

The 10^20 magnitude through the ordinal translation path, at a value that fits neither a 64-bit integer nor a binary64, returning "en-ordinal-one". Pins that the ordinal resolver accepts arbitrary-precision integers rather than narrowing them.

The same digits as a binary64 collapse to 2^53 and select "en-ordinal-two" instead. A JS port that stores placeholder numbers as `number` returns the wrong sentence to a user here; this is the ordinal-path counterpart of the Order-alternative pair, and the only such pair on the generated-placeholder path.

2^53 + 1 delivered exactly to an ordinality-driven generated placeholder, returning "en-ordinal-few". Verified that DefaultStrings.ordinalityForValue is reached: the placeholder's translations map carries ORDINALITY_* keys, which is what selects the ordinal axis. Paired with the double case, this is where losing one unit at the safe-integer boundary changes a returned TRANSLATION rather than a classifier return value.
The control that identifies which form the collapsed double landed on: 2^53 exactly, also "en-ordinal-two". Without it the double case only shows a different answer, not that it is 2^53's answer.

The partner of the exponent-6 case, differing only in the compact exponent and returning "fr-other". Without the pair, a port that dropped the exponent entirely could still pass the exponent-6 row by coincidence.

A compact-decimal placeholder reaching the generated-placeholder resolver. DefaultStrings.cardinalityForValue passes a PluralOperands straight to Cardinality.forOperands, and French `many` fires solely because e = 6, so the oracle records "fr-many". Pins that the caller's operands survive intact instead of being re-derived from a number.
The 10^18 magnitude in a second Indic locale through the translation path ("gu-other"), proving the rule group is shared data rather than reimplemented per locale.

The `n = 1` branch through the translation path, returning "hi-one". Added in review: the identical tagged decimal 1.0 returns "en-other" in the catalog fixture, so this is the only place in the family where one wire value produces two different translations in two locales -- the numeric-equality-versus-visible-places contract stated end to end.

The `i = 0` branch through the translation path: Hindi selects "hi-one" for a value below one, where English selects its `other` form. This is what makes the Indic getResult cases meaningful rather than a uniform `other`.

The Indic `i = 0 or n = 1` family at 10^20 through the translation path ("hi-other"). On its own a port that silently defaulted to `other` when it could not classify would be indistinguishable here -- which is why the 0.5 and 1.0 companion cases exist in the same fixture.

The same digits as a double collapse to 10^18 and select "ru-many" instead of "ru-one". Added in review to replace a 2^53 + 1 Russian double case that could not work: Russian assigns both 2^53 and 2^53 + 1 to `few`, so that collapse was unobservable and the case proved nothing. At 10^18 the collapse is visible in the returned translation.

The exact 10^18 + 1 through generated-placeholder resolution, returning "ru-one". Partner of the double case; together they are the only rows where losing one unit at the 10^18 magnitude changes a returned Russian translation.

The category flips to `one` on a unit that binary64 cannot hold, and the flip is visible in the returned translation ("ru-one" against "ru-many"). This is the end-to-end statement of the whole family.

The same 10^20 classification as the classifier case, but reached through generated-placeholder resolution inside DefaultStrings ("ru-many"). Pins that the translation path builds plural operands from the raw placeholder value rather than from an already-stringified number.
Bengali shares the `i = 0 or n = 1` rule with Hindi. Repeating the family across locales at 10^18 pins that the rule group is shared data, not per-locale code.

Gujarati at 10^20, the third magnitude named by the clause, beyond 64-bit integer range. A port that coerces to `number` before computing i still gets a finite value here, so the real risk this catches is an i derived by string length or by a 64-bit cast.

A compact display of `1` with exponent 17 means 10^17, not 1. PluralOperands' constructor calls movePointRight(compactExponent) BEFORE deriving n/i/v/w/f/t, so the oracle records OTHER. A port that derived n from the mantissa first would find n = 1 and report `one`. This makes that mistake visible in the family the clause names, at the magnitude the clause names.

The same mantissa-shift trap at 10^20, where the shifted value also exceeds binary64 integer precision. Pins that the shift is performed in exact decimal arithmetic rather than by multiplying a double.

Without this case every Indic case in the family returns `other` and none of them proves the rule is `i = 0 OR n = 1` rather than just `n = 1`. 0.5 has a zero integer part, so it takes ONE in Hindi while English calls it `other`. This is the branch the clause is actually about.

The Indic `n = 1` comparison is numeric, not textual: CldrPluralRules compares operands with BigDecimal compareTo, so 1.0 equals 1 even though v = 1, and the oracle records ONE. English calls the identical value `other` because its rule additionally demands v = 0. Pins that a port must compare plural operand values by numeric equality while still tracking visible decimal places separately.

1e17 as a binary64 is exact and reaches BigDecimal through Double.toString, which yields the negative-scale form 1.0E17 and is then stripped to 1E+17. Recorded OTHER, matching the integer path. A port that read the mantissa instead of the expanded value would find n = 1 and report `one`, so this is discriminating despite Hindi's small category set.

The clause names the Indic `i = 0 or n = 1` family at 10^17 specifically. Hindi has only `one` and `other`, so this pins that an 18-digit integer neither has a zero integer part nor equals one (OTHER) -- the trap being an implementation that overflows or truncates i and accidentally produces 0. Meaningful only in combination with the 0.5 and 1.0 rows below, which show the rule is not a constant `other`.

9223372036854775811 is above Long.MAX_VALUE (9223372036854775807), so only an arbitrary-precision integer can carry it. Its last two digits are 11, which English ordinals explicitly exclude from `one`, and the oracle records OTHER. Pins that the n % 100 exclusion is still evaluated exactly at a magnitude no 64-bit integer holds.

The partner of the ...811 case: same magnitude, last two digits 21, so the n % 100 exclusion does not fire and the oracle records ONE. A port computing n % 100 in floating point would produce the same answer for both of these values and fail exactly one of the pair.

9007199254740991 is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. English ordinals key on n % 10 and n % 100, so this value, 2^53 and 2^53+1 land in three different categories -- the only place in the corpus where the three safe-integer boundary values are separable by category alone. Verified against the oracle: ONE. Without it a JS port could round every boundary value to the same double and still look correct.

Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER territory. PluralOperands.Builder.build calls abs() on the value while retaining sourceNumber for expression comparison, so the recorded category is FEW -- the same as the positive twin -- instead of falling through to `other`.
2^53 is the first integer whose successor a binary64 cannot represent. It is itself exact, so this case (TWO) is the control against which the inexact 2^53+1 cases are read.

BigInteger and long reach identical operands for the same integer even though NumberUtils.toBigDecimal builds them by different routes (BigDecimal.valueOf(long).stripTrailingZeros vs new BigDecimal(BigInteger)). Recorded FEW, same as the long row. Without this, a port could implement the exact-integer path with a subtly different digit extraction and never be caught.

The same digits delivered as a binary64. NumberUtils.decimalForDouble routes through Double.toString, which has already collapsed the value to 2^53, so the oracle records TWO -- matching the ...992 case, not the ...993 case. Together with the long case this pins that the TYPE of the caller's value, not its text, decides the operands; a JS port with a single numeric type cannot reproduce both rows.

2^53+1 has no binary64 representation. Carried as an exact integral value its last digit is 3, so the oracle records FEW. A JS port that routes plural input through `number` would see ...992 and pick the n % 10 = 2 category instead; this case is the tripwire that forces bigint/decimal on the classifier path.

thrown.message: Number must be finite, but was Infinity

cases.notes: An explicitly infinite double, the upper end of the magnitude axis this family covers. Reaches the same throw as the 1e400 row, which is the point: the wire input differs (an infinity token rather than an overflowing literal) but the rejection must be identical.

thrown.message: Number must be finite, but was NaN

cases.notes: NaN is the other non-finite binary64 value a JS caller can produce by arithmetic on out-of-range magnitudes. The oracle records IllegalArgumentException("Number must be finite, but was NaN"), so the port rejects it at the same point rather than propagating a NaN through the operand derivation.

thrown.message: Number must be finite, but was Infinity

cases.notes: 1e400 overflows binary64 to Infinity in Java exactly as it does in JavaScript, and NumberUtils.decimalForDouble then throws IllegalArgumentException("Number must be finite, but was Infinity"). Plan section 3.7 requires non-finite numbers to fail when used numerically; a port that parsed the literal exactly instead of overflowing would not throw.

The `1` of the clause's 1 / 1.0 / 1.00 trio, carried as an exact decimal with scale 0 (ONE). Distinct from the corpus's existing integer-1 row because NumberUtils.numberOfDecimalPlaces branches on `instanceof BigDecimal`: this exercises the scale-preserving branch, the integer row the stripTrailingZeros branch.

The `1.00` of the trio. English demands v = 0, so two trailing zeros defeat `one` exactly as one trailing zero does (OTHER). Pins that v counts written places, not significant ones. The `1.0` row of the trio is already in the corpus as classifier.cardinal.trailing-zero-decimal-one-point-zero-is-other-in-en.

The sharpest trailing-zero case in the family: the SAME text `1.0` gives v = 1 as a tagged decimal (already in the corpus, `other`) and v = 0 as a double, because non-BigDecimal numbers are stripTrailingZeros'd in NumberUtils. Recorded ONE. A JS port with one numeric type would give both rows the same answer and fail one of them.

The other direction: an exact integer displayed with two decimal places has v = 2 and is no longer English `one` (OTHER). Pins that visible places are added to the materialized value, not merely reported alongside it.

An explicit visible-decimal-places count overrides the BigDecimal's own scale (PluralOperands.Builder.build sets effectiveScale = visibleDecimalPlaces), so 1.0 becomes v = 0 and English records ONE where the same value without the override records `other`. Pins that the caller's display intent wins over the value's scale.

Latvian is the only CLDR 48.2 rule set reading `v = 2` and `v != 2`, so it is the only place where 0.1, 0.11 and 0.110 are separable by category. This is the v = 1 row: `v != 2 and f % 10 = 1` fires, giving ONE.
The v = 2 row: Latvian `zero` fires on `v = 2 and f % 100 = 11..19`, giving ZERO. Distinguishes exactly two visible decimals from any other count.

The v = 3 row (OTHER), differing from the previous case by a single trailing zero that changes both v and f. Three categories -- one, zero, other -- separated by trailing zeros alone. This is the case that proves 1.0 vs 1.00 style distinctions are observable behavior rather than bookkeeping; without it a port could normalize decimals and still pass everything else in the family.

The same digits as the previous case delivered as a double, which Double.toString normalizes to 0.11 and therefore back to v = 2, recording ZERO instead of OTHER. Pins the type-dependent trailing-zero contract at the one locale where v = 2 is observable.

0.1 displayed with two decimal places is 0.10: v = 2 and f = 10, which the oracle records as OTHER where the same number at its natural scale is ONE. Pins the operand builder's explicit-visible-places path against the natural-scale path in the one locale that can see the difference.

thrown.message: Rounding necessary

cases.notes: Plan section 3.7: reducing visible places throws rather than rounding. The oracle records ArithmeticException("Rounding necessary") from setScale(RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY). A silent round to 2 would change the category and would be invisible in every non-throwing case.
Sinhala `one` includes `i = 0 and f = 1`. f is the fraction digits read as an integer INCLUDING trailing zeros, so 0.1 gives f = 1 and the oracle records ONE.

One trailing zero turns f from 1 into 10 and the category from ONE into OTHER. A port that computed f from the stripped value -- which is what w and t use -- would produce `one` here and never be caught by any locale that only reads v.

THE CONTROL FOR owed-define.refusal.no-translation-no-alternatives. A LocalizedString with NO translation but at least one alternative is legal and builds; the refusal is caused by the CONJUNCTION of both being absent, not by a missing translation on its own. Without this row that refusal could be satisfied by a port that rejected every translation-less string, which would reject the alternatives-only shape the loader accepts -- and that proposition, not coverage, is why the row exists. ABLATION CORRECTION, and the correction is about SCOPE: an earlier note claimed 'removing EITHER row takes LocalizedString#<init>:110 to 3/4, so the two are a matched pair'. Verified by deleting this row from a full-corpus copy and re-running tools/coverage/run.mjs -- 2,817/3,967, byte-identical uncovered set -- with the control ablation firing as it should: deleting the refusal row instead gives 2,816 and puts :110 back at 3/4. The generated-fragment control. MEASURED LOAD-BEARING: removing it takes ExpressionAlternative#equals:1002 and ExpressionTranslation#equals:912 to 1/2 -- the equal arms of the alternative's translation and of the fragment's alternatives list have no other source here. It is ALSO the control for owed-define.refusal.fragment-empty-alternatives: this row reaches the same two-argument ExpressionTranslation constructor with a ONE-element list and builds, so that refusal is attributable to the empty list rather than to the constructor being used at all.

THE SIMPLEST OF THE SIX EQUAL ROWS, and its value is behavioral rather than coverage. MEASURED BY SINGLE-ROW ABLATION: removing it regresses no branch point, because every other row in the family also compares key, translation, commentary and placeholderDefinitions EQUAL at the top level before diverging somewhere deeper, so the not-unequal arms have many sources. What it does supply is an answer of TRUE: without the six equal rows every row here answers contains=false and a port whose equality returned false unconditionally would pass all of them. It also settles a question the corpus could not previously ask -- a LocalizedString built entirely through the public Builder CAN be exactly equal to one the loader produced, so neither the loader nor DefaultStrings' constructor applies hidden normalization.

The range-based control. MEASURED LOAD-BEARING: removing it takes LanguageFormTranslationRange#equals:1090 from covered to 1/2 -- the range END's equal arm has no other source, because owed-define.differs.range-end is the only other row that reaches the end comparison and it takes the unequal arm. LocalizedString#equals:169, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. The extra alternative is APPENDED, so every element the catalog entry has is present and identical and only the arity differs. A port that compared alternatives pairwise up to the shorter list would call these equal, and alternative array order is first-match precedence, so a silently truncated list changes rendering.

LocalizedString#equals:165 -- THE KEY COMPARISON. MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm: with this row removed, :165 sits at 1/2 no matter what else the family contains. The arm cannot be reached at the top level at all, and that is the reason the obvious case does not work: DefaultStrings$LocalizedStringSet.contains looks the candidate up BY the probe's key, so the two keys are equal by construction there, and a probe with a DIFFERENT top-level key gets a null candidate and returns at LocalizedString:140 without comparing anything (ingest.mjs refuses that shape for exactly this reason). But an ALTERNATIVE's key is its expression string -- LocalizedStringLoader.java:2272-2275 passes member.getName() as the child's key -- so a probe whose alternative expression differs descends at :172 and compares unequal keys on the second worklist iteration. Read against owed-define.control.alternatives-equal, which differs only in that expression.

LocalizedString#equals:167, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm: removing this row takes :167 to 1/2. Read against owed-define.control.commented-equal, which differs in this one field. Commentary is TRANSLATOR-FACING metadata that changes no rendered output, so a port that omitted it from equality would be invisible in every other case in the corpus -- and plan v7 section 4.1 names commentary explicitly as part of the model that mergeParsedStringsFiles compares.

ExpressionAlternative#equals:1001, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm; and ONE OF TWO rows that drive ExpressionTranslation#equals:912's unequal arm -- the other is owed-define.differs.fragment-alternative-translation, whose alternatives list is unequal too. An earlier note read as sole ownership of :912; ablation shows this row load-bearing for :1001 only. The expression decides WHEN the alternative fires, so two fragments differing only here render differently for the same input.

ExpressionAlternative#equals:1002, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. Not interchangeable with owed-define.differs.fragment-alternative-expression: the expression comparison short-circuits, so a port comparing only expressions passes that row and fails this one.

ExpressionTranslation#equals:911, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. Read against owed-define.control.fragment-equal: the fragment's DEFAULT translation differs while its alternatives are identical.

LanguageFormTranslation#equals:787, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. Read against owed-define.control.forms-equal: same selector, same form set, one branch TEXT changed. This is the row that says the form map's VALUES are compared and not merely its key set.

LanguageFormTranslation#equals:785, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. Reached through LocalizedString#equals:168. Read against owed-define.control.forms-equal, which differs only in the selector value. The selector NAME decides which caller placeholder drives the branch, so two definitions differing only here render differently for the same input; a port comparing only the branch texts would call them equal.

Same placeholder name, same field TEXTS, different placeholder KIND: the catalog's 'f' is a generated ExpressionTranslation and the probe's is a LanguageFormTranslation. MEASURED load-bearing and NOT interchangeable with owed-define.differs.placeholder-name -- each takes LanguageFormTranslation#equals:780 to 3/4 on its own, because they reach different arms of it: that row reaches the null-argument arm, this one the class-mismatch arm. This is the one shape where a port comparing definitions structurally by their common field names -- both carry a default text and a list-ish tail -- would answer equal. The two kinds are resolved by entirely different code, so calling them equal is a real defect.

The placeholder map's KEY set, at equal size, and MEASURED load-bearing: removing it takes LanguageFormTranslation#equals:780 to 3/4. It reaches the NULL-ARGUMENT arm of that guard, which no other row takes. CORRECTS A PRIOR CLAIM that a differing placeholder name invokes no nested equals because map equality compares key sets first: java.util.AbstractMap.equals does no such thing -- it looks each of the probe's keys up in the candidate's map and compares the value against what it finds, which is null here, so LanguageFormTranslation.equals(null) IS invoked. A port that compared placeholder definitions positionally, or as a bag of values, would call these equal even though the definition is bound to a different name and therefore drives a different placeholder.

LanguageFormTranslationRange#equals:1090, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. Deliberately NOT interchangeable with owed-define.differs.range-start: the start comparison short-circuits, so a port that compared only the start would pass that row and fail this one. The end is what the pair exists to reach.

LanguageFormTranslationRange#equals:1089, MEASURED as the only source of its unequal arm. LanguageFormTranslation#equals:786's unequal arm is supplied by this row AND by owed-define.differs.range-end -- neither is individually load-bearing for it, and the slice's own ablation data says so: removing this row regresses :1089 alone. (An earlier note claimed sole ownership of :786. The reason it gave rules out only the VALUE-based rows, which compare Optional.empty to Optional.empty there and can never take that arm; it does not rule out the other range row.) LocalizedString#equals:166. ABLATION CORRECTION: removing it regresses no branch, because owed-define.control.alternatives-only-builds also takes :166's unequal arm (null translation against 'base'). Read against owed-define.control.alternatives-only-builds and owed-define.control.plain-equal, which supply each half of the conjunction on its own and both build. This is a PROGRAMMATIC construction path: the loader pre-empts it with its own differently-worded message, so no strings file can reach it, and a JS port that exposes a LocalizedString builder must refuse here on its own.
The same extlang subtag under a primary language that is ALSO loaded, so the ladder's choice between the unrecognized original spelling and the recognized collapse is observable as de versus gan.

semanticLanguageRangeForDerivedMatching:2208. extlangEquivalentLanguageRangeFor's shape test with a numeric second subtag: a well-formed language range whose second subtag has the right LENGTH but is not alphabetic, so no extlang equivalence may be derived.

The accepting arm of the same test: ar-ary collapses to ary and the JDK materializes ar-ary as exactly 'ary', so the identity holds and the Moroccan Arabic catalog wins over the generic ar catalog. Without this row, a port that derived NO extlang identities would satisfy the refusal case above.
The control for the row above: the nyn catalog is loaded and exactly reachable, so the refusal there is about the derived extlang identity and not about the catalog being absent.

DefaultStrings.extlangEquivalentLanguageRangeFor:2124, second conjunct. 'no-nyn' has the extlang shape and collapses to 'nyn', which IS a known CLDR language tag -- so the first conjunct passes. The JDK materializes no-nyn as the grandfathered 'nn' instead, so the equivalence must be refused and the nyn catalog must NOT be reachable. Expected: no match. A port that only checked is-known-tag reports a canonical match on nyn.
The alternate order's fallbackLocale as reported by the matcher, so the second channel and the translation channel are both pinned.

The same catalogs and the same unloaded fallback tag with only the tiebreaker order changed; the served catalog must move to hbs. This is what makes the pair prove ORDER is consulted rather than that sh happens to win.

The same resolution observed through the translation itself rather than the match record: the served string must be the sh catalog's. Each catalog carries its own tag as its value, so the answer names the catalog that won.

DefaultStrings.<init>:457 and :459. A port that took the first tiebreaker reports sr-Cyrl here and serves every fallback translation from the wrong catalog.

The control for the row above: same two ranges with depth and weight now agreeing. Its answer must differ from the opposed case, which is what makes that case a discriminator rather than a restatement of 'en-AU wins'.

assignPreferredSpecificHeuristicLocales:2279. Two specific heuristic ranges with recognized depths 3 and 2 and weights in the OPPOSITE order. Depth is consulted before weight, so en-Latn-US claims the tiebreaker-preferred catalog (en-GB) first and en-CA is left en-AU; the governor sweep then selects en-AU because 0.9 is the higher quality. A port whose comparator started with weight gives en-CA the first claim and answers en-GB instead.
The last rung of the same comparator: equal depth AND equal weight fall back to stable request order, so the earlier range claims the tiebreaker-preferred catalog and is served first.

The mirror of the row above. The reported languageRange must follow the request order rather than being fixed at en-us, so an implementation that ordered the comparator's last rung any other way fails exactly one of the pair.
assignPreferredSpecificHeuristicLocales:2283, the rung reached only when depth ties. en-US and en-CA are both recognized-depth 2, so the depth comparison is zero and weight decides the claim order.

Its partner with the fallback outside the candidate set, so nan-CN must be returned. The pair separates 'fallback, then first' from plain 'first' inside the likely-subtag disambiguator specifically -- a different code path from the preferredLocaleForRange pair above.

lookupMatchByLikelySubtag:2623 and :2626. nan-CN and nan-MY share the likely subtag nan-Hans, so both are likely-subtag candidates, but the tiebreaker key is taken from the RANGE's first subtag -- 'zh' -- and the catalogs are keyed under 'nan'. The lookup misses and the configured fallback nan-MY must be preferred over the first candidate nan-CN.

The partner with the fallback moved outside the candidate set: the same lookup misses, the fallback is not a candidate, and the first candidate x-foo-bar must be returned. A port that always returned the first candidate passes this and fails its partner; one that always returned the fallback fails this.

lookupMatchByTiebreakers:2640 (no list for the derived language code), preferredLocaleForRange:2576 (no tiebreaker hit) and :2579 (prefer the configured fallback). Both private-use catalogs match the extended range structurally, the derived lookup key is 'x' and no such language code exists in the tiebreaker map, so the fallback locale x-foo-baz must win over the lexicographically first candidate x-foo-bar.

DefaultStrings.<init>:422, the arm where a language with exactly one loaded catalog DID receive a tiebreaker list. The observable is that construction succeeds and resolution is unchanged; a port that rejected redundant tiebreakers cannot build this fixture at all.
The same instance serving a translation, so 'accepted' is pinned as 'accepted and behaviourally identical to the synthesized identity list' rather than merely 'did not throw'.
The control: the sfb catalog is loaded and exactly reachable, so whatever the row above answers is about the derived semantic range and not about the catalog being absent.

The JDK's lossy rendering of sgn-be-fr requested directly. Pinning it separately keeps the row above from being satisfied by a port that simply hands the range to Locale.forLanguageTag and matches on the result.

semanticLanguageRangeForDerivedMatching:2208, the rung where an already-adopted KNOWN identity must not be displaced by a later UNKNOWN one. The semantic range settles on sfb-x-a, whose CLDR fallback chain reaches the sfb catalog; had the ladder kept the original spelling or taken the trailing sgn-be-fx-x-a alias, neither sfb nor sgn would be reachable.

The same suppression at the broadest request shape, where a bare 'en' has no structural constraint to fall back on either. Paired with the row above so the result cannot be explained by en-US's specificity.

DefaultStrings.languageRangeSpecificityFor:2071, the arm where the AVAILABLE locale has no likely subtag. CLDR maximizes und to en-Latn, which is exactly the requested likely subtag, so the ONLY thing stopping the und catalog from being claimed for an American English request is SupportedLocaleStatics nulling the likely script for undetermined locales. Expected: no match. A port that read the raw likely subtag answers with und.
The control: this fixture is not one where everything answers NONE. fr matches its own catalog exactly, so the two rows above are refusals, not a broken fixture.

One member of each shape in a single list, all at equal weight, with the ordinary member LAST. Java answers fr. A port that computed statics for either special member answers en-US (from und-US, via likely subtag en-Latn) or x-lokal-a (from x-lokal, via prefix truncation) instead, so this row separates the arms twice over. FINDING recorded while authoring it: this list cannot cover the private-use conjunct of DefaultStrings$MemberStatics.<init>:3051, because CldrLocaleData.TagParts.forLanguageTag sets privateUse=true only on its startsWith("x-") early return, and that same return sets language="" -- so privateUse implies undetermined and the third conjunct is unreachable in the true direction. That disposition is now excluded, not owed.

The guard against overcorrecting: withholding the canonical/fallback-chain precomputation must not make a private-use range unmatchable. The exact spelling of the loaded private-use catalog still selects it EXACTLY, so a port that answered NONE for every private-use range fails here while passing the two rows above.

A wildcard-free PRIVATE-USE range. Every private-use range already in the corpus (x-*, x-foo-*) carries a wildcard, so nothing had shown what a bare one does. DISCRIMINATION: a private-use member gets no canonicalRange, no canonicalRangeSubtags, no fallbackChainCanonicalTags, no requestedLikelyLanguageScript and semanticDepth 0 (DefaultStrings$MemberStatics.<init>:3051 else arm), which structurally disables every derived rung. A port that computed those statics would hold canonicalRangeSubtags [x, lokal] and reach the loaded x-lokal-a catalog by prefix truncation, exactly as en reaches en-US. Java selects nothing.

The positive half of the same discrimination, so the observable difference is a SELECTION rather than an absence: the private-use member is listed FIRST at equal weight and Java still selects fr. A port that derived a match for x-lokal from canonical statics would answer x-lokal-a instead.

An undetermined range with a REGION attached, which is where the withheld statics bite hardest: CLDR's likely subtag for und-US is en-Latn, so a port that computed requestedLikelyLanguageScript and the fallback chain for this member would reach the loaded en-US catalog. Java computes none of them and selects nothing. The corpus's only prior undetermined range (und-latn) is bare, so nothing had shown that the undetermined refusal survives an attached region that would otherwise resolve.

Bidi is the option whose per-call override is most visible in the output text. The instance leg is ALWAYS, which isolates even an LTR request, so a port that treats the present-but-null bidiIsolation key as an override to the RTL_LOCALES default emits the placeholder WITHOUT isolation marks while Java still isolates it. The isolation characters are in the recorded translation, so the two arms differ character for character.

All four nullable behaviour keys present and null at once, with no locale: the whole options object must be indistinguishable from passing none. Java reaches TranslationOptions.Builder.build() with every field null and returns TranslationOptions.none(), so the ambient instance locale en and the instance ALWAYS isolation both survive. Any port that lets one of the four present-undefined keys through as an override changes the output -- isolation marks disappear, the handler or policy is displaced, or the call is refused for naming two locale sources.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Absent.Key' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: The ONLY input shape that reaches TranslationOptions.Builder.build()'s all-fields-null shortcut (TranslationOptions.java:385), which returns the shared TranslationOptions.none() instead of constructing an options object. Every other corpus case sets at least one field, so the last of that line's ten outcomes was untaken and a port could treat an all-undefined options object as something other than 'no options' while passing all 1,965 cases. The discriminating half is the instance handler: a per-call handler REPLACES the instance one (DefaultStrings.java:683-685), so a port that keys on KEY PRESENCE rather than on a non-null VALUE installs `undefined` as the handler here and returns the key 'Absent.Key' instead of the instance handler's 'INSTANCE-HANDLER-TEXT'. No per-call locale, so the ambient instance locale en is used.

An explicitly null failure-handler key on a fixture with no instance handler, so the case runs against a port that has not implemented handler ingress. Java's Builder.translationFailureHandler is documented @Nullable and null means 'no override' (TranslationOptions.java:361-365), so the lookup is an ordinary successful one. A port that validates the key's presence rather than its value rejects a call it should have accepted.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Absent.Key' for locale 'en'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [en]

cases.notes: The same present-but-null handler key, this time alongside a real per-call locale so the options object is genuinely constructed rather than collapsing to none(). Separates the two propositions: 'an all-undefined options object is no options' (the sibling case) from 'an explicitly undefined handler key does not replace the instance handler'. A port that conflates them passes one and fails the other.

failures.message: Unable to resolve translation key 'Items.EnOnly' for locale 'ru'. Reason: MISSING_TRANSLATION. Attempted locales: [ru]

cases.notes: The strongest discriminator in this family. The instance policy is `never`, which halts at the ru candidate on a plain MISSING_TRANSLATION instead of falling back to en. A port that reads a present-but-null translationFallbackPolicy as 'no per-call policy was set, so use the library default' -- or as 'replace the instance policy with the default missing-or-no-match' -- continues to en and returns 'en:only-here'. Java keeps the instance policy and produces the halted result. Compare ingress-matrix.policy.instance-never-halts-on-missing-translation, which is the same request with the key absent entirely.

The fallback-policy mirror of owed-null-options.handler.explicit-null-on-a-plain-fixture, on the same instance-option-free fixture. Java's Builder.translationFallbackPolicy is documented @Nullable with null meaning 'no override' (TranslationOptions.java:377-381); the lookup succeeds at en. Together the two cases pin that every @Nullable per-call option key accepts an explicit no-value without changing the outcome, which is the runtime half of the port's structural TranslationOptions union.

TranslationOptions refuses to hold a locale and language ranges at once (TranslationOptions.java:70-71). In Java the builder makes that state unconstructible; in JS TranslationOptions is a caller-written structural union, so '{ locale, localeMatch: undefined }' is an ordinary caller shape and the mutual exclusion becomes a RUNTIME check. This pins that an explicitly undefined range key is ABSENT, not a second locale source: the lookup is locale-driven and resolves in ru. A port implementing the exclusion as a crude 'both keys present' test refuses this call. The reverse shape -- an explicitly null locale alongside real ranges -- is not expressible through the oracle, because VectorOracle.optionsFrom reads the locale with JsonObject.getString, which throws on a present JSON null rather than returning the default.

The same proposition as owed-null-options.ranges.explicit-null-alongside-a-locale-is-not-both-sources, restated on a fixture that carries no instance handler, policy, supplier or limits, so a port that has not yet implemented those capabilities still RUNS it instead of having it absorbed as unsupported. A locale with an explicitly null range key is a locale-only lookup: en resolves to 'Checkout'. A port implementing TranslationOptions' mutual exclusion (TranslationOptions.java:70-71) as a 'both keys present' test refuses the call; a port that lets the null range key displace the locale answers with the fr fallback 'Paiement'.

The partner arm of the same guard: the later member's range IS the representative's semantic range, so the election fires and the materialized alias supplies derived matching. It differs from the row above in one subtag spelling only, which is what attributes any behavioral difference between them to the third conjunct rather than to how the preference group was formed.

Reference leg 1, and the row that makes the combined header below discriminating. 'sgn-NO' alone is a RECOGNIZED tag, so matchFor:1618 skips the election for it and it supplies its own derived matching: its likely language-script is nsi-Latn, so it selects the nsi catalog. Recorded rather than asserted -- this is the answer a port that elects the materialized alias would also give for the two-member header, which is why that answer would be wrong there and right here.

Reference leg 2. 'sgn-nsl' alone is UNRECOGNIZED; its lossless extlang equivalent nsl is its independently established semantic range, whose likely language-script is nsl-Latn, so it selects the nsl catalog. The two reference legs select DIFFERENT catalogs, which is what gives the two-member row below a decidable outcome.

DefaultStrings.matchFor:1621-1624, the semantic-member election, in the arm where the representative is RETAINED. The two members form one preference group -- their JDK identity sets both contain sgn-no -- so the later member joins the earlier as representative; the representative is unrecognized and its semantic range is nsl, but the later member's range is 'sgn-NO', which is NOT that semantic range, so the third conjunct is false and derived matching must stay with the representative. DISCRIMINATION: this row must answer the same catalog as owed.m3b.aliasgroup.sgn-nsl-alone and NOT the one owed.m3b.aliasgroup.sgn-no-alone answers. A port that handed derived matching to any materialized alias in the group would follow sgn-NO to nsi-Latn -- exactly the 'crossing conflicting JDK/CLDR alias data' the source comment forbids -- and would still pass both reference legs. Equal weights are deliberate: an unequal weight makes the later member inactive at matchFor:1612 and the election is never reached.
The isolating partner, so the private-use answer is read against a locale that DOES maximize to an RTL script under the same fixture.
The LTR partner that maximizes. Together the three pin that 'no likely subtag' behaves like LTR rather than like RTL or like a failure.
